parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -бѣ́съ (-bě́sŭ), calque of Ancient Greek -μανής (-manḗs) and -μαργος (-margos). Cognate with беси́ться (besítʹsja, “to rage”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -бѣ́сїе (-bě́sije), calque of Ancient Greek -μανία (-manía) and -μάργος (márgos). Cognate with беси́ться (besítʹsja, “to rage”).

parole.significato: Combining form used to form prefixed perfective verbs, with the approximate meaning "to turn".
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вратити (vratiti), from Proto-Slavic *vortiti; doublet of inherited вороти́ть (vorotítʹ)

parole.significato: Combining form used to form prefixed perfective verbs with various meanings, e.g. "to reward" or "to block".
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic градити (graditi), from Proto-Slavic *gorditi.

parole.significato: used to form past passive participles from verbs in -ить (-itʹ) and -еть (-etʹ), which are frequently lexicalized into…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -еньнъ (-enĭnŭ), from енъ (enŭ) + ьнъ (ĭnŭ). Originally used to form adjectives from past passive participles in Old Church Slavonic, later reinterpreted as a past passive participle suffix within the Russian literary language. Compare the native past participle suf

parole.significato: Used to form adjectives from nouns or sometimes other adjectives, often relational (meaning "related to X"); a variant…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -ьскъ (-ĭskŭ), from Proto-Slavic *-ьskъ. Doublet of -ский (-skij).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -жды (-ždy), from Old Church Slavonic шьды (šĭdy), from Proto-Slavic *šьdъ. Compare with Russian шедший (šedšij) and шедши (šedši), forms of идти (idti).

parole.significato: forms relational and possessive adjectives from nouns describing animals and people: -'s, -ine, -ian
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -ии (-ii), further from Proto-Slavic *-ьjь, whose native descendant *-ей (*-jej) was displaced (compare и́ней (ínej) [ˈinʲɪj] from Proto-Slavic *jьnьjь and пыре́й (pyréj) [pɨˈrʲej] from Proto-Slavic *pyrьjь).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -ыи (-yi), displaced expected -ой (-oj) in unstressed positions, from Proto-Slavic *-ъ + *jь, doublet of -о́й (-ój).

parole.significato: forms adjectives from verbs, verbal nouns and compounds: -ous, -al, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -ии (-ii), displaced native *-ей (*-jej) (compare и́ней (ínej) from Proto-Slavic *jьnьjь), from Proto-Slavic *-jьjь.

parole.significato: Combining form used to form imperfectives of derived perfectives of ложи́ть (ložítʹ).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -лагати (-lagati), from Proto-Slavic *lagati, iterative of *ložiti.

parole.significato: Suffix used to form neuter nouns from verbs, usually denoting a place and sometimes having an archaic or literary feel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -лище (-lište). Equivalent to -ло (-lo) + -ище (-išče).

parole.significato: -ish, -ic, -al, -ed; having a particular quality of, pertaining to, associated with; forms adjectives from nouns, and s…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -ьныи (-ĭnyi), from Proto-Slavic *-ьnъjь. Doublet of -ной (-noj).

parole.significato: Suffix used to form adjectives from verbs.
parole.testo: Derives from the gerundive (причастодѣтїе (pričastodětije)) suffix found in late Old Church Slavonic -тельно, -тельнѣ (-telĭno, -telĭně).

parole.significato: Combining form used to form prefixed imperfective verbs with the approximate meaning "ask", "pull".
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тѧѕати (tędzati), from Proto-Slavic *tędzati. Doublet of native тяга́ть (tjagátʹ) without the Slavic progressive palatalization applied.

parole.significato: Combining form used to form prefixed perfective verbs with various meanings, e.g. "to steal" or "to lift".
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic хꙑтити (xytiti), from Proto-Slavic *xytiti. Related to хвата́ть (xvatátʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -ыи (-yi), displaced expected -ой (-oj) in unstressed positions, from Proto-Slavic *-ъ + *jь, doublet of -о́й (-ój).

Inherited from Old East Slavic абие (abije, “now, suddenly”), from Old Church Slavonic абиѥ (abije, “now, immediately”), from Proto-Slavic *abьje. Compare Sanskrit अह्नाय (ahnāya, “instantly, at once”), Ancient Greek ἄφαρ (áphar, “at once”), ἄφνω (áphnō, “suddenly”), possibly from a Proto-Indo-Europ
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic агньць (agnĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *agnьcь, a derivative of *àgnę; eventually from Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʷn-. Compare native ягнёнок (jagnjónok).

parole.significato: hell, Hades (the abode of the damned)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic адъ (adŭ), from Old Church Slavonic адъ (adŭ), from Ancient Greek ᾍδης (Hāídēs).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic азъ (azŭ), from Proto-Slavic *(j)azъ.

Inherited from Old East Slavic азъбукꙑ (azŭbuky); borrowed from Old Church Slavonic азъбоукꙑ (azŭbuky), from the names of the first two letters of the Cyrillic alphabet, азъ (azŭ) + боукꙑ (buky), a calque of Ancient Greek ἀλφάβητος (alphábētos).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic азъ (azŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic акы (aky).

parole.significato: to crave, to thirst (for), to be greedy
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic алъкати (alŭkati), from Proto-Slavic *olkati. Doublet of лака́ть (lakátʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic алъчьнъ (alŭčĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *òlčьnъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *álˀkinas.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic амъвонъ (amŭvonŭ), from Ancient Greek ἄμβων (ámbōn).

parole.significato: antichrist (someone that works against the teachings of Christ)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic антихристъ (antixristŭ), from Old Church Slavonic антихрьстъ (antixrĭstŭ), from Koine Greek ἀντίχριστος (antíkhristos).

Inherited from Old East Slavic апостолъ (apostolŭ), from Old Church Slavonic апостолъ (apostolŭ), from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓πόστολος (ăpóstolos), from ἀποστέλλω (apostéllō, “I send off”), from ἀπό- (apó-, “from”) and στέλλω (stéllō, “I set”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic апостольскъ (apostolĭskŭ). By surface analysis, апо́стол (apóstol) + -ский (-skij).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic армѣнинъ (arměninŭ), рамѣнинъ (raměninŭ), from Ancient Greek Ἀρμένιος (Arménios, “Armenian”).
From Old Church Slavonic арханг҄елъ (arxangʹjelŭ), and Ancient Greek ἀρχᾰ́γγελος (arkhắngelos).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic архисѵнаго́гъ (arxisünagógŭ), from Ancient Greek ἀρχισῠνᾰ́γωγος (arkhisŭnắgōgos). By surface analysis, архи- (arxi-) + Ancient Greek συνάγωγος (sunágōgos, “synagogue”).
From Old Church Slavonic аспида (aspida), from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓σπίς (ăspís), ᾰ̓σπῐ́δος (ăspĭ́dos, “asp”).

parole.significato: to grow/turn crimson/purple, to redden, to flush
parole.testo: From Old Church Slavonic багрити (bagriti, “to redden, to become scarlet-coloured/colored”), from Old Church Slavonic багръ (bagrŭ, “purple”), from Proto-Slavic *bagrъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₁- (“to heat up; bathe”). Cognates include English bake, German bähen (“to bake”) and Anci

From Old Church Slavonic баснословити (basnosloviti, “to tell tales”), calque of Ancient Greek μυθολογέω (muthologéō, “to tell tales”). By surface analysis, ба́сня (básnja, “fable”) + -о- (-o-) + сло́во (slóvo, “word”) + -ный (-nyj).
From беда́ (bedá) + -ство (-stvo) + -ие (-ije) or from Old Church Slavonic бѣдьство (bědĭstvo), remodeled after other slavonicisims featuring -ствие (-stvije).

parole.significato: to live in poverty, to be in misery
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бѣдьствовати (bědĭstvovati). By surface analysis, бе́дствие (bédstvije) + -овать (-ovatʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic безбожиѥ (bezbožije). By surface analysis, без- (bez-) + бог (box) + -ие (-ije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic безбожьникъ (bezbožĭnikŭ). By surface analysis, без- (bez-) + бог (box) + -ник (-nik).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic безбожьнъ (bezbožĭnŭ), a calque of Ancient Greek ᾰ̓́θεος (ắtheos). By surface analysis, без- (bez-) + бог (box) + -ный (-nyj)
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic безмлъвиѥ (bezmlŭvije). By surface analysis, без- (bez-) + молва́ (molvá) + -ие (-ije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic безмлъвьнъ (bezmlŭvĭnŭ). By surface analysis, без- (bez-) + молва́ (molvá) + -ный (-nyj)
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic безмлъвьствовати (bezmlŭvĭstvovati). By surface analysis, безмо́лвие (bezmólvije) + -ствовать (-stvovatʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic безмѧтежьнъ (bezmętežĭnŭ). Equivalent to без- (bez-) + мяте́ж (mjatéž) + -ный (-nyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic безобразиѥ (bezobrazije). By surface analysis, без- (bez-) + о́браз (óbraz) + -ие (-ije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бездръпътьнъ (bezdrŭpŭtĭnŭ). By surface analysis, без- (bez-) + ро́пот (rópot) + -ный (-nyj)
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic безоумьѥ (bezumĭje), which is a calque of Ancient Greek ἀφροσύνη (aphrosúnē). By surface analysis, без- (bez-) + ум (um) + -ие (-ije).

parole.significato: to rage, to rave, to be possessed
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бѣсьновати сѧ (běsĭnovati sę). By surface analysis, (obsolete) бе́сный (bésnyj) + -ова́ть (-ovátʹ) + -ся (-sja); see беснова́тый (besnovátyj).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic беспрѣстаньнъ (besprěstanĭnŭ, “ceaseless, incessant”), from Old Church Slavonic беспрѣстани (besprěstani, “ceaselessly, incessantly”). By surface analysis, бес- (bes-) + престан- (prestan-) + -ный (-nyj), based on a combining stem of преста́ть (prestátʹ, “to cease,
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic биѥниѥ (bijenije). By surface analysis, бить (bitʹ) + -ение (-enije). Compare native битьё (bitʹjó).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бисьръ (bisĭrŭ, “pearls”), from Bulgar, from Arabic بُسْر (busr, “unripe dates”) from the root ب س ر (b s r) related to things being early, so applied to pearls because unripe dates can have some tactile and optical properties similar to pearls.
Inherited from Old East Slavic благо (blago), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благо (blago), from Proto-Slavic *bolgo. Displaced the inherited East Slavic form бо́лого (bólogo)
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благо- (blago-), a calque of Ancient Greek εὐ- (eu-). Bound form of благо́й (blagój), by surface analysis, благо́й (blagój) + -о- (-o-).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благоволити (blagovoliti). By surface analysis, бла́го (blágo) + -о- (-o-) + во́ля (vólja) + -и́ть (-ítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благовон҄ьнъ (blagovonʹĭnŭ). By surface analysis, благово́ние (blagovónije) + -ный (-nyj).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благоговѣйный (blagogovějnyj). By surface analysis, благо- (blago-) + гове́й- (govéj-, “to respect”, obsolete) + -ный (-nyj). Compare Ukrainian благогові́йний (blahohovíjnyj).

parole.significato: to revere, to venerate, to be in awe of
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благоговѣти (blagogověti). By surface analysis, бла́го (blágo) + -о- (-o-) + гове́ть (govétʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благодар҄еньѥ (blagodarʹjenĭje). By surface analysis, благодари́ть (blagodarítʹ) + -е́ние (-énije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благодарити (blagodariti). By surface analysis, бла́го (blágo) + -о- (-o-) + дари́ть (darítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благодарьствьнъ (blagodarĭstvĭnŭ). By surface analysis, благодари́ть (blagodarítʹ) + -ство (-stvo) + -енный (-ennyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic [Term?]

parole.significato: full of divine grace, godsent, God-given
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благодатьнъ (blagodatĭnŭ). By surface analysis, благода́ть (blagodátʹ) + -ный (-nyj).

parole.significato: divine grace, boon, bliss (a blessing or benefit)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благодать (blagodatĭ). By surface analysis, бла́го (blágo) + -о- (-o-) + дать (datʹ) + -ь (-ʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благодьньствие (blagodĭnĭstvije). By surface analysis, бла́го (blágo) + -о- (-o-) + день (denʹ) + -ство (-stvo) + -ие (-ije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благодѣтел҄ь (blagodětelʹĭ), itself a calque of εὐεργέτης. By surface analysis, бла́го (blágo) + -о- (-o-) + деть (detʹ) + -тель (-telʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благодѣꙗньѥ (blagodějanĭje). By surface analysis, бла́го (blágo) + -о- (-o-) + дея́ние (dejánije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благъ (blagŭ). Displaced the inherited East Slavic form, from Proto-Slavic *bolgъ (“good”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благолѣпьнъ (blagolěpĭnŭ), a calque of Ancient Greek εὐπρεπής (euprepḗs). By surface analysis, бла́го (blágo) + -о- (-o-) + ле́пый (lépyj) + -ный (-nyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благообразьнъ (blagoobrazĭnŭ). By surface analysis, бла́го (blágo) + -о- (-o-) + о́браз (óbraz) + -ный (-nyj).

parole.significato: well-being, prosperity, welfare (state of health, happiness and/or prosperity)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благополоучиѥ (blagopolučije). By surface analysis, благо- (blago-) + получи́ть (polučítʹ) + -ие (-ije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благоприѧтьнъ (blagoprijętĭnŭ). By surface analysis, бла́го (blágo) + -о- (-o-) + прия́тие (prijátije) + -ный (-nyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благородьѥ (blagorodĭje). By surface analysis, бла́го (blágo) + -о- (-o-) + род (rod) + -ие (-ije).

parole.significato: noble, aristocratic, wellborn (of the nobility, of the high-born class, especially in Russia before 1917)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благородьнъ (blagorodĭnŭ). By surface analysis, бла́го- (blágo-, “good”) + род (rod, “birth”) + -ный (-nyj).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благословениѥ (blagoslovenije). By surface analysis, благослови́ть (blagoslovítʹ) + -е́ние (-énije). Compare Ukrainian благослове́ння (blahoslovénnja), Belarusian благаславе́нне (blahaslavjénnje).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благословенъ (blagoslovenŭ). By surface analysis, благослове́ние (blagoslovénije) + -ный (-nyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благословити (blagosloviti), a calque of Ancient Greek ἐυλογεῖν (eulogeîn). By surface analysis, бла́го- (blágo-, “good”) + сло́во (slóvo) + -и́ть (-ítʹ, “word”).

parole.significato: gift, donation; charity; good deed, benefaction
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благостꙑни (blagostyni). Equivalent to благость (blagostʹ) + -иня (-inja).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благоѫханиѥ (blagoǫxanije), a calque of Ancient Greek εὐωδία (euōdía). By surface analysis, благоуха́ть (blagouxátʹ) + -а́ние (-ánije).

parole.significato: to be fragrant, to smell sweet
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благоѫхати (blagoǫxati), a calque of Ancient Greek εὐωδέω (euōdéō), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *ǫxati. By surface analysis, благо- (blago-) + уха́ть (uxátʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благочьстивъ (blagočĭstivŭ), a calque of Ancient Greek εὐσεβής (eusebḗs). By surface analysis, благо- (blago-) + чести́ть (čestítʹ, “to honor”) + -и́вый (-ívyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благочьстьѥ (blagočĭstĭje), a calque of Ancient Greek εὐσέβεια (eusébeia). By surface analysis, благо- (blago-) + чести́ть (čestítʹ, “to honor”) + -ие (-ije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic блаженъ (blaženŭ), passive participle of блажити (blažiti), from Proto-Slavic *bolžiti, from *bolgo or *bolgъ, of unknown origin.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic блаженьство (blaženĭstvo). By surface analysis, блаже́нный (blažénnyj) + -ство (-stvo).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic блато (blato), from Proto-Slavic *bolto. Doublet of боло́то (bolóto).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic блюсти (bljusti), from Proto-Slavic *bľusti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *bjaustei, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ-.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic блюститель (bljustitelĭ). By surface analysis, блюсти́ (bljustí) + -тель (-telʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бога дѣлꙗ (boga dělja, “for God's sake”).

parole.significato: church service, divine service, public worship, worship service
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Old Church Slavonic Богослꙋженіе (Bogosluženije), analyzable as бог (bog, “God”) + -о- (-o-) + служение (služenije, “service, worship”), influenced by the usage of Ancient Greek λατρεία (latreía) in the New Testament.

parole.significato: to worship, to deify, to idolize, to adore
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic боготворити (bogotvoriti), a calque of Ancient Greek θεοποιέω (theopoiéō). By surface analysis, бого- (bovo-) + творить (tvoritʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic божьство (božĭstvo), a calque of Ancient Greek θεότης (theótēs). By surface analysis, бог (bog, “god”) + -ество́ (-estvó).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic болѣзнь (bolěznĭ), from Proto-Slavic *bolěznь. By surface analysis, боле́ть (bolétʹ) + -знь (-znʹ).

Inherited from Old East Slavic боꙗринъ (bojarinŭ), from Old Church Slavonic болꙗринъ (boljarinŭ), from Bulgar, attested in Greek variously as βωυλε, βοιλας, βοηλας, βουληα, βοιλᾶς, βολιᾶς. The form with -j- might have come from contamination with Old East Slavic бои (boi).
Inherited from Old East Slavic брада (brada), itself a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic брада (brada), from Proto-Slavic *borda. Doublet of борода́ (borodá), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бразда (brazda), from Proto-Slavic *borzda. Doublet of борозда́ (borozdá), the inherited East Slavic form.

Inherited from Old East Slavic брозда (brozda, “bridle, horse bit”), from Old Church Slavonic бръзда (brŭzda), from Proto-Slavic *brъzda, further origin uncertain: perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrusdʰos, but a complicated Slavic etymology has also been proposed.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бракъ (brakŭ), from Proto-Slavic *borkъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic брань (branĭ), from Proto-Slavic *bornь. Compare the inherited Old East Slavic боронь (boronĭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic брашьно (brašĭno), from Proto-Slavic *boršьno. Doublet of бо́рошно (bórošno), the inherited East Slavic form.
Inherited from Old East Slavic брѣгъ (brěgŭ), from Old Church Slavonic брѣгъ (brěgŭ) / ⰱⱃⱑⰳⱏ (brěgŭ), from Proto-Slavic *bergъ. Akin to the inherited doublet бе́рег (béreg).

Inherited from Old East Slavic брѣмѧ (brěmę), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic брѣмѧ (brěmę), from Proto-Slavic *bermę (“load, burden”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH-men-. Compare the inherited doublet бере́мя (berémja).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic брьньнъ (brĭnĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *brьnьnъ.

parole.significato: existence, being (the state of being, existing, or occurring)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бꙑтиѥ (bytije), from Proto-Slavic *bytьje, from Proto-Slavic *byti. Doublet of бытьё (bytʹjó), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ваꙗньѥ (vajanĭje, “sculpture, idol”). By surface analysis, вая́ть (vajátʹ) + -я́ние (-jánije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ваꙗтель (vajatelĭ). By surface analysis, вая́ть (vajátʹ) + -тель (-telʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ваꙗти (vajati), from Proto-Slavic *vajati, possibly related to Old Church Slavonic вити (viti), Russian вить (vitʹ).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въвръгнѫти (vŭvrŭgnǫti), въврѣщи (vŭvrěšti), calque of Ancient Greek ἐμβάλλω (embállō). By surface analysis, в- (v-) + -ве́ргнуть (-vérgnutʹ). Compare Latin iniciō and German hineinwerfen for the semantics.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въдъхновениѥ (vŭdŭxnovenije), which itself is probably a calque of Greek ἔμπνοια (émpnoia, “inspiration”). Compare typologically Latin īnspīrō (whence инспири́ровать (inspirírovatʹ)); ве́яние (véjanije), наве́ять (navéjatʹ), навева́ть (navevátʹ) (< веять (vejatʹ)),
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вѣжда (věžda), from Proto-Slavic *věďa. Displaced Old East Slavic вѣжа (věža).

parole.significato: majesty (the quality of being impressive and great)

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въспрѧнѫти (vŭspręnǫti). By surface analysis, вос- (vos-) + пря́нуть (prjánutʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въславити (vŭslaviti). By surface analysis, вос- (vos-) + сла́вить (slávitʹ).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въстокъ (vŭstokŭ, “rising, east”), displacing the native East Slavic form всток (vstok) (preserved in some dialects); the Old Church Slavonic term is a calque of Ancient Greek ἀνατολή (anatolḗ, “rising, east”). By surface analysis, вос- (vos-) + ток (tok), formally
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въстръгъ (vŭstrŭgŭ), a deverbal of въстръгати (vŭstrŭgati).

parole.significato: to delight, to enrapture, to ravish
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въстръгати (vŭstrŭgati), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *tъrgati.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въсточьнъ (vŭstočĭnŭ). By surface analysis, восто́к (vostók) + -ный (-nyj).

parole.significato: to enrapture, to delight, to ravish
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въсхытити (vŭsxytiti, “to fascinate, to snatch away”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въсходъ (vŭsxodŭ). Doublet of всход (vsxod). Сompare восходи́ть (vosxodítʹ) and всходи́ть (vsxodítʹ).

parole.significato: to ascend, to climb, to go up, to mount
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въсходити (vŭsxoditi). By surface analysis, вос- (vos-) + ходить (xoditʹ). Doublet of всходи́ть (vsxodítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вътъще (vŭtŭšte).

parole.significato: henceforth, henceforward, from now on, in future, for the future
parole.testo: From Old Church Slavonic прѣдъ (prědŭ, “before, in front of”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врагъ (vragŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vorgъ. Compare the inherited doublet во́рог (vórog, “enemy, foe”) (poetic).

parole.significato: enmity, hostility, animosity, antagonism (hostile or unfriendly disposition)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вражьда (vražĭda), from Proto-Slavic *voržьda (the Old East Slavic form is found in the poetic Ukrainian ворожда (vorožda)), from *vorgъ + *-ьda. Cognate with Polish wróżda, Czech vražda.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врата (vrata), from Proto-Slavic *vorta. Doublet of воро́та (voróta), the inherited East Slavic form.

parole.significato: therapist, not surgeon, not hospital nurse
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врачь (vračĭ), from Proto-Slavic *vьračь. By surface analysis, врать (vratʹ) + -ач (-ač). Originally meant "witch-doctor, enchanter".

parole.significato: to revolve, to rotate, to turn
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вращати (vraštati), from Proto-Slavic *vorťati, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wert-, whence English vertex, versatile, worth and -ward. Doublet of воро́чать (voróčatʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врѣдъ (vrědŭ), from Proto-Slavic *verdъ. Doublet of ве́ред (véred), the inherited East Slavic form.

parole.significato: to injure, to harm, to hurt, to damage, to cause damage
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врѣдити (vrěditi). from Proto-Slavic *verditi. By surface analysis, вред (vred) + -и́ть (-ítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врѣдьнъ (vrědĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *verdьnъ. By surface analysis, вред (vred) + -ный (-nyj).
Inherited from Old East Slavic врѣменьнъ (vrěmenĭnŭ), from Old Church Slavonic врѣменьнъ (vrěmenĭnŭ). By surface analysis, вре́мя (vrémja) + -ный (-nyj).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врѣмѧ (vrěmę), from Proto-Slavic *vermę < *vertmen, from Proto-Indo-European *wertmen. Displaced native Old East Slavic веремѧ (veremę). Cognate with Sanskrit वर्त्मन् (vártman, “track, course”). See also pleophony (CeRC > CeReC) and liquid metathesis (CeRC > CReC,
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въсадьникъ (vŭsadĭnikŭ). By surface analysis, в- (v-) + садить (saditʹ) + -ник (-nik).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въселенаꙗ (vŭselenaja, “the inhabited world, ecumene”). Doublet of вселённая (vseljónnaja).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въселеньскъ (vŭselenĭskŭ). By surface analysis, вселе́н(ная) (vselén(naja)) + -ский (-skij)
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въсоуѥ (vŭsuje), from Proto-Slavic *sujь (“futile”).
в (v) + туне (tune), from Old Church Slavonic тоуне (tune), from Proto-Slavic *tuňь. Compare with Slovene stunja.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic выспрьнъ (vysprĭnŭ), from выспрь (vysprĭ).
Inherited from Middle Russian вы́ꙗ (výja), from Old East Slavic вꙑ́ꙗ (výja), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вꙑꙗ (vyja), from Proto-Slavic *vyja.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вѧщии (vęštii), from Proto-Slavic *vęťьjь. Displaced Old East Slavic вѧчии (vęčii).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic г҄еона (gʹjeona), from Ancient Greek γέεννᾰ (géennă).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic генварь (genvarĭ), генуарии (genuarii), from Byzantine Greek Γενάρης (Genárēs), Ἰανουάριος (Ianouários), from Latin Iānuārius, from Latin Iānus (“god in Rome mythology”), from (perhaps) Proto-Indo-European *ei- (“to go”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic глава (glava), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic глава (glava). Doublet of голова́ (golová), the regular East Slavic reflex. Compare typologically Latin capitāneus (whence капита́н (kapitán)) < caput (whence also шеф (šef)). Also compare typologically Latin capitulum (

parole.significato: chief, leading, main, principal, head, central
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic главьнъ (glavĭnŭ), ultimately, from Proto-Slavic *golvьnъ. Parsable as глава́ (glavá) + -ный (-nyj). Doublet of головно́й (golovnój).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic глаголъ (glagolŭ), from Proto-Slavic *golgolъ (“speech, word”). In the sense "verb" introduced by Meletius Smotrytsky as a calque of Latin verbum. Displaced the native Russian *гологол (*gologol), still found in голого́лить (gologólitʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гладъ (gladŭ), from Proto-Slavic *goldъ. Doublet of го́лод (gólod), the inherited East Slavic form.
Inherited from Old East Slavic гласъ (glasŭ), itself a learned borrowing from Old Church Slavonic, not exhibiting pleophony as opposed to the inherited doublet го́лос (gólos).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гласити (glasiti), from Proto-Slavic *golsiti. By surface analysis, глас (glas) + -и́ть (-ítʹ). Doublet of голоси́ть (golosítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гласьнъ (glasĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *golsьnъ. By surface analysis, глас (glas, “voice”) + -ный (-nyj). The phonetic sense is a semantic loan from Latin vōcālis.

parole.significato: herald, spokesman, town crier, mouthpiece (person who used to make proclamations to the common folk, before the develop…
parole.testo: From Old Church Slavonic глашатаи (glašatai, “herald”), itself from Proto-Slavic *golšatajь (“herald”), a compound of *golšati (“to speak”) and *-ajь (“deverbal suffix”). By surface analysis, гласи́ть (glasítʹ) + -а́тый (-átyj).

parole.significato: to disdain, to abhor, to shun, to loathe
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гнушати сѧ (gnušati sę), from Proto-Slavic *gnušati. By surface analysis, гну́с(ный) (gnús(nyj)) + -а́ть (-átʹ) + -ся (-sja).

parole.significato: town, city, used as a common city name suffix (Волгоград, Калининград, Ленинград)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic градъ (gradŭ), which is a reflex of Proto-Slavic *gȏrdъ. Doublet of го́род (górod), which was normally inherited by pleophony. Old Church Slavonic word shows liquid metathesis characteristic of South Slavic area.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гражданинъ (graždaninŭ), from Proto-Slavic *gorďaninъ. Compare native горожа́нин (gorožánin), which was inherited from Old East Slavic. Related to го́род (górod, “city”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic грькъ (grĭkŭ), from Old Church Slavonic грькъ (grĭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *grьkъ. By surface analysis, back-formation from гре́цкий (gréckij).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic грѣхопадениѥ (grěxopadenije). By surface analysis, грех (grex) + -о- (-o-) + паде́ние (padénije).
Inherited from Old East Slavic грьчьскъ (grĭčĭskŭ), from Old Church Slavonic грьчьскъ (grĭčĭskŭ), from Proto-Slavic *grьčьskъ. See also гре́ческий (gréčeskij).

parole.significato: to come, to begin (of time, period, event)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic грѧсти (gręsti), from Proto-Slavic *gręsti (“to go”). Cognate with Latin gradior, Gothic 𐌲𐍂𐌹𐌳 (grid, “step”), English progress, congress, ingress, grade.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гоубител҄ьнъ (gubitelʹĭnŭ). By surface analysis, губи́ть (gubítʹ) + -тельный (-telʹnyj).

parole.significato: in order to, in order that, so that
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic да бꙑ (da by). By surface analysis, да (da) + бы (by).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дебелъ (debelŭ), from Proto-Slavic *debelъ. Compare native dialectal дебёлый (debjólyj) and Belarusian дзябёлы (dzjabjóly).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дѣиствиѥ (děistvije). By surface analysis, де́йство (déjstvo) + -ие (-ije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дѣиство (děistvo). By surface analysis, де́ять (déjatʹ) + -ство (-stvo).

parole.significato: to do an action or activity
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дѣиствовати (děistvovati). By surface analysis, де́йство (déjstvo) + -овать (-ovatʹ).

Inherited from Old East Slavic декѧбрь (dekębrĭ), from Old Church Slavonic декѧбр҄ь (dekębrʹĭ), from Byzantine Greek Δεκέμβριος (Dekémbrios). Ultimately from Latin december, from decem + Latin -ber, from -bris, an adjectival suffix.

parole.significato: brazen, impudent, impertinent, insolent, cheeky, pert
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дрьзъкъ (drĭzŭkŭ), as *дёрзкий (*djórzkij) would be expected, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *dьrzъkъ. By surface analysis, де́рзый (dérzyj) + -кий (-kij).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дрьзость (drĭzostĭ), as *дёрзость (*djórzostʹ) would be expected. By surface analysis, де́рзый (dérzyj) + -ость (-ostʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic длань (dlanĭ). Doublet of ладо́нь (ladónʹ), the inherited Old East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic доблѥстьнъ (dobljestĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *dobľestьnъ. By surface analysis, до́блесть (dóblestʹ) + -ный (-nyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic доблѥсть (dobljestĭ), from Proto-Slavic *dobľestь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic добродѣтѣль (dobrodětělĭ), a calque from Ancient Greek εὐεργεσία (euergesía)). By surface analysis, до́брый (dóbryj) + -о- (-o-) + деть (detʹ) + -ель (-elʹ).
Possibly from Old Church Slavonic довълъ (dovŭlŭ) or Old East Slavic довлѣ (dovlě). Compare довле́ть (dovlétʹ).

parole.significato: sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic довлѣетъ дневи ѕлоба егѡ (dovlějetŭ dnevi dzloba ego), from the Church Slavonic text of Matthew 6:34, corresponding to дово́льно для ка́ждого дня свое́й забо́ты (dovólʹno dlja káždovo dnja svojéj zabóty) in the Russian Synodal Bible and to sufficient unto the day is

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic довьлѣти (dovĭlěti), from Proto-Slavic *dovьlěti. The second sense appeared in the late 19th century and is not connected with the original; it arose by association with дави́ть (davítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic длъготрьпѣниѥ (dlŭgotrĭpěnije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic достоиновѣрьнъ (dostoinověrĭnŭ), a calque of Ancient Greek ἀξιόπιστος (axiópistos). By surface analysis, досто- (dosto-) + ве́рный (vérnyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic драгъ (dragŭ), from Proto-Slavic *dorgъ. Doublet of дорого́й (dorogój).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дрѣво (drěvo). Doublet of де́рево (dérevo), the inherited Old East Slavic form.
PIE word  *dʰugh₂tḗr Borrowing from Old Church Slavonic дъщи (dŭšti). Doublet of дочь (dočʹ).

parole.significato: dyak, clerk, official in Russia in the 14th-17th centuries
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic диꙗкъ (dijakŭ), from Ancient Greek διάκος (diákos). Compare another meaning development from the source: Czech žák (“pupil; disciple”). Akin to дья́кон (dʹjákon). Compare typologically Latin clēricus (whence клерк (klerk)), from Ancient Greek κληρικός (klērikós), wh
From еди́ный (jedínyj, “united; unified; one; single”), from Old Church Slavonic ѥдинъ (jedinŭ). Doublet of оди́н (odín, “one”) and одно- (odno-, “uni-”).
From еди́ный (jedínyj, “united; unified; one; single”), from Old Church Slavonic ѥдинъ (jedinŭ).
Derived from Old Church Slavonic ѥдинъ (jedinŭ) + -ый (-yj). By surface analysis, един- (jedin-) + -ый (-yj). Related to Russian оди́н (odín, “one”).

parole.significato: once a ... (occurring once in a given time period)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic иже (iže) (whence Russian и́же (íže)), from Proto-Slavic *jь že.

parole.significato: litany, suffrage (one of a number of prayer petitions that make up most of the worship in the Orthodox Church)
parole.testo: From Old Church Slavonic ектенїѧ (ekteniję), from Ancient Greek ἐκτένεια (ekténeia).
From Old Church Slavonic ѥлѣи (jelěi), from Byzantine Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “oil”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic єпархиꙗ (eparxija), borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐπαρχία (eparkhía).

parole.significato: letter "ъ", now called твёрдый знак (tvjórdyj znak)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ѥръ (jerŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic еретикъ (eretikŭ), from Ancient Greek αἱρετικός (hairetikós).

parole.significato: letter "ь", now called мя́гкий знак (mjáxkij znak)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ѥрь (jerĭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic естьствьнъ (estĭstvĭnŭ). By surface analysis, естество́ (jestestvó) + -енный (-ennyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic естьство (estĭstvo), which is a calque of Ancient Greek οὐσία (ousía). By surface analysis, есть (jestʹ, “there is”) + -ество́ (-estvó).

parole.significato: echidna (any of the four species of small spined monotremes)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic ехидьна (jexidĭna, “venomous snake”), from Old Church Slavonic ѥхидьна (jexidĭna), from Ancient Greek ἔχιδνα (ékhidna, “viper, snake”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жѩжда (žjęžda), from Proto-Slavic *žęďa, from *žędati + *-ja. Displaced native Old East Slavic жажа (žaža).

parole.significato: to thirst (for), to crave (for), to hunger (for)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жѧждати (žęždati). By surface analysis, жажда (žažda) + -ать (-atʹ). Compare Ukrainian жада́ти (žadáty).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жьзлъ (žĭzlŭ), from Proto-Slavic *žezlъ. Doublet of native dialectal жезе́л (žezél).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жрьтва (žrĭtva), from Proto-Slavic *žьrtva (“sacrifice”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *girʔ-, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷrH-. The inherited form would be *жёртва (*žórtva).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic животьноѥ, животьно (životĭnoje, životĭno), the nominative neuter singular of Old Church Slavonic животьнъ (životĭnŭ). See живо́тный (živótnyj).

parole.significato: vital (relating to or characteristic of life), life
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жизньнъ (žiznĭnŭ). By surface analysis, жизнь (žiznʹ) + -енный (-ennyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жизнь (žiznĭ), from Proto-Slavic *žiznь. By surface analysis, жить (žitʹ) + -знь (-znʹ). Compare Old Polish żyźń.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жилище (žilište). By surface analysis, жить (žitʹ, “to live, to reside”) + -ли́ще (-líšče)
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic житиѥ (žitije, “life”), from Proto-Slavic *žitьje, from Proto-Slavic *žiti (“to live”). Doublet of житьё (žitʹjó), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жрѣбии (žrěbii), from Proto-Slavic *žerbьjь. Doublet of же́ребей (žérebej), the inherited East Slavic form.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жоупелъ (župelŭ) (alternative form: зюпелъ (zjupelŭ)), from Old High German swebal or sweval, from Proto-Germanic *sweblaz. An alternative etymology, which explains the presence of оу, derives жоупелъ (župelŭ) from Latin sulpur, possibly via a Rhaeto-Romance or othe
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic забъвениѥ (zabŭvenije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic [Term?]; has the form of a past active participle. Compare заблуди́ться (zabludítʹsja, “to get lost”), заблужда́ться (zabluždátʹsja, “to err, to be mistaken”).

parole.significato: to bequeath, to leave, to will
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic завѣщати (zavěštati), from Proto-Slavic *zavěťati.
From Old Church Slavonic заклати (zaklati, “to stab”); doublet of the inherited East Slavic word заколо́ть (zakolótʹ).

parole.significato: to imprint (in), to impress (in), to engrave (in)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic запечатьлѣти (zapečatĭlěti). By surface analysis, за- (za-) + -печатле́ть (-pečatlétʹ)
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic запрѣтити (zaprětiti, “to forbid”). By surface analysis, за- (za-) + прети́ть (pretítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic запрѣщати (zaprěštati). By surface analysis, запрет- (zapret-) + -а́ть (-átʹ).

parole.significato: to defend, to guard, to protect
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic защитити (zaštititi). By surface analysis, за- (za-) + щит (ščit) + -ить (-itʹ).

parole.significato: to defend, to guard, to protect
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic защищати (zaštištati). By surface analysis, защити́ть (zaščitítʹ) + -а́ть (-átʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic зьданиѥ (zĭdanije). By surface analysis, здать (zdatʹ) + -ание (-anije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съдравьѥ (sŭdravĭje), from Proto-Slavic *sъdorvьje. By surface analysis, здра́вый (zdrávyj) + -ие (-ije). Doublet of здоро́вье (zdoróvʹje).

From imperative form of здравствовать (zdravstvovatʹ, “to be well, to prosper”), from adjective здравый (zdravyj) borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съдравъ (sŭdravŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sъdorvъ of unclear origin.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съдравъ (sŭdravŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sъdorvъ. Doublet of здоро́вый (zdoróvyj), the inherited Old East Slavic form.

parole.significato: mirror or similar reflective surface (e.g. of a river)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic зрьцало (zrĭcalo), from Proto-Slavic *zьrcadlo. Compare Polish zwierciadło, Serbo-Croatian зр̀цало / Serbo-Croatian zr̀calo. Doublet of native зе́ркало (zérkalo).

parole.significato: herb, grass, cereal, graminoid (type of grass)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic злакъ (zlakŭ), from Proto-Slavic *zolkъ. The hypothetical East Slavic inherited form *золокъ (*zolokŭ) is unattested.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic злато (zlato), from Proto-Slavic *zolto, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃-. Doublet of зо́лото (zóloto).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic зълокъзньнъ (zŭlokŭznĭnŭ). By surface analysis, зло- (zlo-) + козни (kozni) + -ный (-nyj)

parole.significato: vindictive, rancorous, unforgiving, likely to hold a grudge
parole.testo: From Middle Russian злопамятной (zlopamjatnoj), from Old East Slavic злопомнити (zlopomniti, “to remember evil”). Likely from an unattested Old Church Slavonic form calquing Ancient Greek μνησίκακος (mnēsíkakos). By surface analysis, зло (zlo, “evil”) + па́мять (pámjatʹ, “memory”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic зълополоучьнъ (zŭlopolučĭnŭ), a calque of Ancient Greek κακότυχος (kakótukhos). By surface analysis, злой (zloj) + -о- (-o-) + получи́ть (polučítʹ) + -ный (-nyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic змии (zmii), from Proto-Slavic *zmь̀jь. Doublet of змей (zmej), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic зракъ (zrakŭ), from Proto-Slavic *zorkъ. Doublet of зо́рок (zórok), the inherited East Slavic form.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ибо (ibo). By surface analysis, univerbation of и (i) + бо (bo), which is a calque from Ancient Greek καὶ γάρ (commonly used in Ancient Greek since the conjunction γάρ (gár, “because”) cannot appear first in a sentence). Compare или (ili) for similar derivation.
From Old East Slavic, from Old Church Slavonic игоумєнъ (igumenŭ), from Byzantine Greek ἡγούμενος (hēgoúmenos).
From иждиви́ть (iždivítʹ, “to spend”) + -е́ние (-énije), from Old Church Slavonic иждити (ižditi), derived from *из-жити. See из- (iz-), жить (žitʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic иже (iže), from Proto-Slavic *jь že.

parole.significato: izhe, Church Slavonic name of the Cyrillic letter и
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic иже (iže).

parole.significato: to rid, to save, to relieve
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic избавити (izbaviti). By surface analysis, из- (iz-) + -ба́вить (-bávitʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic избѣгати (izběgati). By surface analysis, из- (iz-) + бе́гать (bégatʹ) + -а́ть (-átʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic избѣгнѫти (izběgnǫti). By surface analysis, из- (iz-) + -бе́гнуть (-bégnutʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic избѣжати (izběžati). By surface analysis, из- (iz-) + бежа́ть (bežátʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic избꙑтъкъ (izbytŭkŭ), from Old Church Slavonic избꙑти (izbyti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic изваꙗти (izvajati). By surface analysis, из- (iz-) + вая́ть (vajátʹ).

parole.significato: to extract, to elicit, to draw out
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic извлѣщи (izvlěšti). By surface analysis, из- (iz-) + влечь (vlečʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic извратити (izvratiti). By surface analysis, из- (iz-) + -врати́ть (-vratítʹ, “to turn”), Doublet of извороти́ть (izvorotítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic извращати (izvraštati), from Proto-Slavic *jьzvorťati. By surface analysis, из- (iz-) + враща́ть (vraščátʹ, “to turn”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic извращьньць (izvraštĭnĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *jьzvorťьnьcь. By surface analysis, изврат (izvrat) + -енец (-enec).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic измъжденъ (izmŭždenŭ), past passive participle of измъждити (izmŭžditi). Related to мозжи́ть (mozžítʹ, “to ache dully but persistently”), мо́зглый (mózglyj, “dank; frail”), dialectal мо́згнуть (mózgnutʹ, “to spoil, to perish”), мзга (mzga, “wet weather”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic изнести (iznesti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic изобрѣсти (izobrěsti), which is probably a calque of Ancient Greek εξευρίσκω (exeurískō, “to invent”). By surface analysis, из- (iz-) + обрести́ (obrestí).

parole.significato: to invent (design a new process or mechanism)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic изобрѣтати (izobrětati), which is probably a calque of Ancient Greek εξευρίσκω (exeurískō, “to invent”). By surface analysis, изобрет- (izobret-) + -а́ть (-átʹ).
From изобрет- (izobret-) + -е́ние (-énije) or borrowed directly from Old Church Slavonic изобрѣтениѥ (izobrětenije).

parole.significato: to cultivate, to refine, to make perfect
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic изощрити (izoštriti, “to sharpen”).

parole.significato: to amaze, to astound, to astonish, to strike (to fill with surprise)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic изоумѣти (izuměti). By surface analysis, из- (iz-) + ум (um) + -ить (-itʹ). Originally meant "to make mad".
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic изѧти (izęti), from Proto-Slavic *jьzъjęti. By surface analysis, из- (iz-) + ять (jatʹ). Cognate with Polish zdjąć.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic изимати (izimati), from Proto-Slavic *jьzimati. By surface analysis, из- (iz-) + ыма́ть (ymátʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic изѧщьнъ (izęštĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *jьzętjьnъ. Compare Czech vzácný (“precious”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic или (ili). By surface analysis, univerbation of и (i) + ли (li).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic имушть (imuštĭ), present active participle of имѣти (iměti).
From Old Church Slavonic инако (inako) (from *jьnako (“otherwise, differently”)) + мысль (myslʹ) + -ие (-ije).

parole.significato: person belonging to a different tribe or nation
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic иноплємєньникъ (inoplemenĭnikŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ѵпакои́ (üpakoí), from Ancient Greek ὑπακοή (hupakoḗ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ѵпокри́тъ (üpokrítŭ), from Ancient Greek ῠ̔ποκρῐτής (hŭpokrĭtḗs, “actor, hypocrite”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic исказити (iskaziti). By surface analysis, ис- (is-) + кази́ть (kazítʹ).

parole.significato: since olden times, from of old, from time immemorial
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic искони (iskoni), from Proto-Slavic *jьz koni.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic исконьнъ (iskonĭnŭ). By surface analysis, искони́ (iskoní) + -ный (-nyj)
Inherited from Old East Slavic искусъ (iskusŭ), which was borrowed from Old Church Slavonic искусъ (iskusŭ).

parole.significato: to experience, to acquire knowledge of
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic искоусити (iskusiti). By surface analysis, из- (iz-) + куси́ть (kusítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic искоусьнъ (iskusĭnŭ). By surface analysis, искуси́ть (iskusítʹ) + -ный (-nyj).

parole.significato: to experience, to acquire knowledge of
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic искоушати (iskušati). By surface analysis, искуси́ть (iskusítʹ) + -а́ть (-átʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic исповѣдь (ispovědĭ) or испове́дать (ispovédatʹ) + -ь (-ʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic испраздьнити (isprazdĭniti), from Proto-Slavic *jьzporzdьniti.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic исступлениѥ (isstuplenije), a calque of Ancient Greek ἔκστασις (ékstasis, “ecstasy”, literally “out of step”), from ис- (is-) (compare Russian ис- (is-, “out”)) and ступлениѥ (stuplenije) (compare Russian ступи́ть (stupítʹ, “to step”)).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic истина (istina), from Proto-Slavic *jьstina, from *jistъ. Compare Latvian īstens (“real, true, genuine”).

parole.significato: to annihilate, to destroy, to eradicate, to exterminate (to reduce to nothing)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic истрѣбити (istrěbiti). Morphologically, из- (iz-) + тре́ба (tréba) + -ить (-itʹ).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic истѧѕати (istędzati). By surface analysis, ис- (is-) + -тяза́ть (-tjazátʹ) (akin to тяга́ть (tjagátʹ), via PIE akin to тяну́ть (tjanútʹ)). Compare typologically му́чить (múčitʹ) (akin to мя́гкий (mjáxkij), мягчи́ть (mjaxčítʹ)), Latin torqueō, tortus (whence English
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic исчезати (isčezati) or ищезати (ištezati), from Proto-Slavic *jьzčezati.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic исчезновениѥ (isčeznovenije) or ищезновениѥ (išteznovenije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic исчезнѫти (isčeznǫti), from Old Church Slavonic чезнѫти (čeznǫti), from Proto-Slavic *čeznǫti. The inherited form would be *исчёзнуть (*isčóznutʹ).

From Old Church Slavonic июнии (ijunii), from Byzantine Greek Ἰούνιος (Ioúnios), from Latin iūnius, from Iūnō (“Juno”), from (perhaps) Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuHn̥ḱós, from *h₂óyu (“vital force, youthful vigor”).

parole.significato: a vigil lamp; a cresset, usually hanging and richly decorated, containing a floating wick fed by oil, which is placed b…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic канъдило (kanŭdilo), from Ancient Greek κανδήλη (kandḗlē), from Latin candela (“candle”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic канонъ (kanonŭ), from Old Church Slavonic канонъ (kanonŭ), from Ancient Greek κανών (kanṓn).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic капище (kapište, “idol; pagan temple”), from капь (kapĭ, “image”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic каѳисма (kaθisma), from Byzantine Greek κάθισμα (káthisma).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic качьство (kačĭstvo), from как (kak). Compare Latin quālitās from quālis.

parole.significato: Caesar (title of a Roman or Byzantine emperor)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кесарь (kesarĭ), from Koine Greek Καῖσαρ (Kaîsar), itself a borrowing from Latin Caesar. Doublet of ка́йзер (kájzer), царь (carʹ), це́зарь (cézarʹ), and це́сарь (césarʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic китъ (kitŭ), from Ancient Greek κῆτος (kêtos).

parole.significato: fount, treasury, storehouse (abundant, inexhaustible source of something, e.g. knowledge)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кладѧѕь (kladędzĭ, “well”), from Proto-Slavic *kòldędzь; compare the inherited doublet коло́дезь (kolódezʹ).

parole.significato: only used in меч-кладене́ц (meč-kladenéc, “a mythical sword with special powers”)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic *кладѣньць (*kladěnĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *koldenьсь (“stabber, sword of stabbing type”). Related to Proto-Celtic *kladiwos (“stabber, sword of stabbing type”), Proto-Slavic *kolti (“to stub”). Native East Slavic *колоденьць > Russian: *колоденец.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic класъ (klasŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kolsъ. Doublet of ко́лос (kólos), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic клевета (kleveta), from Proto-Slavic *kleveta.

parole.significato: to slander, to calumniate, to libel
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic клеветати (klevetati), from Proto-Slavic *klevetati.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic клеврѣтъ (klevrětŭ), from Vulgar Latin collivertus, from Latin collibertus.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic клирикъ (klirikŭ), Ancient Greek κληρῐκός (klērĭkós) or κλῆρος (klêros).

parole.significato: guileful, insidious, perfidious, crafty, treacherous, scheming
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic коварьнъ (kovarĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kovarьnъ. Related to кова́ть (kovátʹ), ко́зни (kózni).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ковьчегъ (kovĭčegŭ) from Middle Mongol ᠬᠠᠤᠷᠴᠠᠭ (qaurčaɣ) presumably through a Turkic language. Compare Mongolian хуурцаг (xuurcag).

Plural of кознь (koznʹ, “intrigue, plot, machination”), further, borrowed from Old Church Slavonic къзнь (kŭznĭ), from Proto-Slavic *kъznь, from *kovati (“to forge”), whence also Old Church Slavonic ковати (kovati, “to forge, to plot”) and Russian кова́ть (kovátʹ, “to forge”). Akin to кова́рный (kov
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic количьство (količĭstvo), from колико (koliko) + -ьство (-ĭstvo), which is a calque of Ancient Greek ποσότης (posótēs). Compare Latin quantitas.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic коловратъ (kolovratŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kolovortъ. Doublet of inherited коловоро́т (kolovorót). Revived by neo-pagan leader Alexey Dobrovolsky in the 1990s in reference to the symbol he made up.

From Old Church Slavonic кольце (kolĭce), a diminutive from коло n (kolo, “wheel, circle”) + -ьце (-ĭce, suffix forming diminutives of neuters), the former from Proto-Slavic *kȍlo (“wheel”), whence Russian колесо́ (kolesó, “wheel”).

parole.significato: helmsman (he who is responsible for steering a ship)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кръмьчии (krŭmĭčii). By surface analysis, корма́ (kormá) + -чий (-čij); the helm or rudder was usually in the stern of the ship. Compare корми́ло (kormílo, “helm, rudder”).

parole.significato: oblique (placed or moving at an angle)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic косвенъ (kosvenŭ), from the equivalent of Russian косо́й (kosój) + -енный (-ennyj), ultimately, from Proto-Slavic *kosvenъ (“indirect”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic коснѫти сѧ (kosnǫti sę), Proto-Slavic *kosnǫti sę.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic късьнъ (kŭsĭnŭ, “slow, late”), from Proto-Slavic *kъsьnъ. Compare Bulgarian къ́сно (kắsno, “late”), Serbo-Croatian ка̏сно (“late”), Slovene kəsȃn (“careless, slow, late”) (feminine kəsnà), also kəsə̀n. Further cognate with Lithuanian kùšlas (“frail, wretched”) (also
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic крамола (kramola), from Proto-Slavic *kormola. Displaced native Old East Slavic коромола (koromola).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кратъ (kratŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kortъ. Cognate with Serbo-Croatian -кра̄т (e.g. два́кра̄т (“twice”)), Slovene kràt (gen. kráta), Czech -krát (e.g. dvakrát (“twice”)), Slovak krát, Polish -kroć (e.g. dwakroć (“twice”)), Upper Sorbian -kroć, Lower Sorbian -krot. Mor
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кратъкъ (kratŭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kortъkъ. Doublet of коро́ткий (korótkij).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic крьстъ (krĭstŭ), from Proto-Slavic *krьstъ. Doublet of Христо́с (Xristós) and крёст (krjost), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кромѣщьнъ, кромѣшьнъ (kroměštĭnŭ, kroměšĭnŭ). By surface analysis, кро́ме (króme) + -е́шный (-éšnyj)
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кротость (krotostĭ), from Proto-Slavic *krotostь.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic коумиръ (kumirŭ), whose origin is uncertain. Perhaps a Turkic or Semitic borrowing: compare Classical Syriac ܟܘܡܪܐ (kūmrāʾ, “priest”), whence Old Armenian քուրմ (kʻurm, “priest”). Has also been connected to Ossetian гуымиры (g°ymiry, “giant”) and Georgian გმირი (gmi
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кѫпѣль (kǫpělĭ), from Proto-Slavic *kǫpělь. Related to купа́ть (kupátʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кѫща (kǫšta), from Proto-Slavic *kǫťa. Doublet of ку́ча (kúča), the inherited East Slavic form still found in dialects.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ланита (lanita), from Proto-Slavic *olnita. Cognate with Bulgarian ланита (lanita). Non-Slavic cognates include Gothic 𐌰𐌻𐌴𐌹𐌽𐌰 (aleina), Latin ulna (“elbow”), Sanskrit अणि (aṇi, “the point of a needle”).
Derived from Old Church Slavonic лѣствица (lěstvica), from Proto-Slavic *lěstva, from *lězti (“to climb”) + *-tv-. Doublet of ле́стница (léstnica).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic лъжесъвѣдѣтельство (lŭžesŭvědětelĭstvo), a calque of Ancient Greek ψευδομαρτυρία (pseudomarturía). By surface analysis, лже- (lže-) + свиде́тельство (svidételʹstvo).

parole.significato: to rejoice (at, over), to triumph (over), to exult (at, in)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ликовати (likovati), from Proto-Slavic *likovati, from *likъ (“round dance”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic лиходѣй (lixoděj), from лихо (lixo, “bad”) + дѣꙗти (dějati, “to do”), from Proto-Slavic *lixodějь. By surface analysis, ли́хо (líxo, “evil”) + -о- (-o-) + -дей (-dej, “doer”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic лицемѣрити (liceměriti), from Old Church Slavonic лицемѣрити (liceměriti). Compare Ukrainian лицемі́рити (lycemíryty). Can also be analysed as лицо́ (licó, “face”) + -е- (-e-) + ме́рить (méritʹ, “measure”)
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic любьзнъ (ljubĭznŭ).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic маи (mai) from Byzantine Greek Μάϊος (Máïos) from Latin māius from Maia (perhaps) from Proto-Indo-European *magya (“she who is great”) from Proto-Indo-European *mégh₂s (“great”).
From Old Church Slavonic мантиꙗ (mantija), from Latin mantum.
Analyzable as ма́сло (máslo, “oil, butter”) + -и́на (-ína); borrowed from Old Church Slavonic маслина (maslina), from Proto-Slavic *maslo.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мьгновениѥ (mĭgnovenije), from Proto-Slavic *mьgnovenьje, from *mьgnǫti (“to blink”), from *migati (“to blink”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic междоу (meždu). Compare inherited East Slavic меж (mež).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мрьзъкъ (mrĭzŭkŭ), native form would be *мёрзкий (*mjórzkij), from Proto-Slavic *mьrzъkъ (“frosty, cold”). Cognate to мёрзнуть (mjórznutʹ), моро́з (moróz).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мрьзость (mrĭzostĭ), native form would be *мёрзость (*mjórzostʹ). By surface analysis, ме́рз(кий) (mérz(kij)) + -ость (-ostʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мрьтвьнъ (mrĭtvĭnŭ).

parole.significato: to shimmer, to twinkle, to glimmer, to flicker
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мрьцати (mrĭcati), from Proto-Slavic *mьrcati. Doublet of native dialectal мерка́ть (merkátʹ), also compare смерка́ться (smerkátʹsja).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мьчьта (mĭčĭta), from Proto-Slavic *mьčьta, from *mikati + *-ьta.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мьчьтаниѥ (mĭčĭtanije). By surface analysis, мечта́ть (mečtátʹ) + -а́ние (-ánije).

parole.significato: to dream (to imagine something, usually intensely but often unrealistically desired; to desire, hope or assume such a t…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мьчьтати (mĭčĭtati), from Proto-Slavic *mьčьtati.

parole.significato: alms, handout (something given to the poor as charity)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic милостꙑн҄и (milostynʹi, “mercy”), from Proto-Slavic *milostyni. By surface analysis, ми́лость (mílostʹ, “mercy”) + -ыня (-ynja).

From Old Church Slavonic мигдалъ (migdalŭ) possibly through Polish migdał, from Latin amygdalus, from Greek ἀμύγδαλος (amýgdalos), ἀμυγδάλη (amygdáli), ἀμυγδάλιον (amygdálion), of Semitic origin. Cognate with Belarusian мігда́л (mihdál), German Mandel, Romanian migdal, Ukrainian мигда́ль (myhdálʹ).
Inherited from Old East Slavic миротворьць (mirotvorĭcĭ), from Old Church Slavonic. By surface analysis, мир (mir) + -о- (-o-) + твори́ть (tvorítʹ) + -е́ц (-éc).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic митрополиꙗ (mitropolija), from Byzantine Greek μητρόπολις (mētrópolis).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic младьньць (mladĭnĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *moldenьcь. By surface analysis, младо́й (mladój) + -енец (-enec).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic младъ (mladŭ), from Proto-Slavic *moldъ (“young”). Doublet of молодо́й (molodój).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic младость (mladostĭ), doublet of мо́лодость (mólodostʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic млатъ (mlatŭ), from Proto-Slavic *moltъ. Doublet of мо́лот (mólot), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic млѣко (mlěko), from Proto-Slavic *melko. Doublet of молоко́ (molokó), the inherited Old East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic млѣчьнъ (mlěčĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *melčьnъ. By surface analysis, мле́ко (mléko) + -ный (-nyj). Doublet of моло́чный (molóčnyj).

parole.significato: wish for longevity, many years (of prosperity, health, etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мъногаꙗ лѣта (mŭnogaja lěta). Cognate with Ukrainian мно́гая лі́та (mnóhaja líta). Cf. modern Russian мно́гие го́ды (mnógije gódy), мно́го лет (mnógo let) or less commonly мно́гие ле́та (mnógije léta).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мъножьство (mŭnožĭstvo), from Proto-Slavic *mъnožьstvo, from *mъnogъ (“much, many”) + *-ьstvo. By surface analysis, мно́гий (mnógij) + -ество (-estvo).
Borrowed from Russian Old Church Slavonic монахъ (monaxŭ), from Ancient Greek μοναχός (monakhós, “monk, (originally) solitary”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мощи (mošti), plural of мошть (moštĭ), from Proto-Slavic *mogťi. Cognate to мощь (moščʹ), мочь (močʹ).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мощь (moštĭ), from Proto-Slavic *moťь. Compare native мочь (močʹ) and Ukrainian міч (mič) (both inherited from Old East Slavic мочь (močĭ)) and Ukrainian міць (micʹ) and Belarusian моц (moc) (both borrowed from Polish moc).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мразъ (mrazŭ), from Proto-Slavic *morzъ. Doublet of моро́з (moróz), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мракъ (mrakŭ), from Proto-Slavic *morkъ. Doublet of мо́рок (mórok), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мраморъ (mramorŭ), from Proto-Slavic *mormorъ, a borrowing from Latin marmor. Displaced the inherited Old East Slavic мороморъ (moromorŭ).

parole.significato: to darken, to cover with gloom
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мрачити (mračiti), from Proto-Slavic *morčiti. By surface analysis, мрак (mrak) + -и́ть (-ítʹ). Doublet of моро́чить (moróčitʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мрачьнъ (mračĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *mȍrčьnъ. Analyzable as мрак (mrak) + -ный (-nyj). Doublet of мо́ро́чный (móróčnyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мрѣжа (mrěža), from Proto-Slavic *merža. Doublet of мерёжа (merjóža), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic муринъ (murinŭ), ultimately from Latin Maurus. Cognates include Polish Murzyn, Ukrainian му́рин (múryn), Belarusian му́рын (múryn). Doublet of мавр (mavr).

parole.significato: mutiny, rebellion (armed uprising often comprising disloyal soldiers)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мѧтєжь (mętežĭ), from Proto-Slavic *mętežь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мѧтежьникъ (mętežĭnikŭ). By surface analysis, мяте́ж (mjatéž) + -ник (-nik).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мѧтежьнъ (mętežĭnŭ). Equivalent to мяте́ж (mjatéž) + -ный (-nyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic наблюдати (nabljudati). Equivalent to на- (na-) + блюда́ть (bljudátʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic наваждениѥ (navaždenije), from Old Church Slavonic навадити (navaditi).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic надежда (nadežda), from Proto-Slavic *nadeďa. Doublet of надёжа (nadjóža), the inherited East Slavic form.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic надъменъ (nadŭmenŭ, “inflated, blown up”), from Proto-Slavic *nadъmenъ (“inflated, blown up”) - passive past participle of *nadǫti (“inflate, blow up”). Doublet of наду́тый (nadútyj) and до́мна (dómna).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic наитие (naitije); constructed as if найти́ (najtí) + -тие (-tije).

parole.significato: to impose, to inflict (opinions, penalties, prohibitions, punishments, requirements, taxes)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic налагати (nalagati). By surface analysis, на- (na-) + -лага́ть (-lagátʹ). Compare it's neutral counterpart накла́дывать (nakládyvatʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic насладити сѧ (nasladiti sę). By surface analysis, на- (na-) + слади́ть (sladítʹ, “to sweeten”) + -ся (-sja)
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic наслаждати сѧ (naslaždati sę). By surface analysis, наслади́ться (nasladítʹsja) + -а́ть (-átʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic наслаждениѥ (naslaždenije). By surface analysis, наслади́ться (nasladítʹsja) + -е́ние (-énije).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic *настоѩщь (*nastojęštĭ), present active imperfective participle of настоꙗти (nastojati, “to happen; to approach (of time)”). Compare настоѩщиꙗ жизнь (nastojęštija žiznĭ, “this life, this world”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic насѫщьнъ (nasǫštĭnŭ).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic начѧло (načęlo), from Proto-Slavic *načędlo. By surface analysis, нача́ть (načátʹ) + -ло (-lo), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ken- (“new, fresh”), whence English recent and ceno-.

parole.significato: chief, boss, superior, master, principal, commander
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic начѧльникъ (načęlĭnikŭ). Also analyzable as нача́ло (načálo) + -ник (-nik). Cognate with Czech náčelník, Polish naczelnik, Serbo-Croatian načelnik, and Ukrainian начальник (načalʹnyk).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic нашьствиѥ (našĭstvije), нашествиѥ (našestvije). By surface analysis, наше́д (našéd) + -ствие (-stvije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic небеса (nebesa).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic небо (nebo), from Proto-Slavic *nebo. Doublet of нёбо (njóbo), the inherited East Slavic form.
From небре́чь (nebréčʹ) + -ный (-nyj), from Old Church Slavonic небрѣщи (nebrěšti). Compare native Russian бе́режный (bérežnyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic небꙑтиѥ (nebytije). By surface analysis, не- (ne-) + бытие (bytije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic невѣжда (nevěžda), from Proto-Slavic *nevěďa (“ignorant person < ignorance”), from *ne- + *věďa, from *věděti (“to know”). Doublet of неве́жа (nevéža).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic негодовати (negodovati), from Proto-Slavic *negodovati (“to be indignant”), related to *godìti (“to please”).

parole.significato: malaise, malady, illness, feebleness (especially of old or sick people), sickness
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic немощь (nemoštĭ). Doublet of не́мочь (némočʹ), the inherited form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic непрѣмѣньнъ (neprěměnĭnŭ). Compare inherited переме́нный (pereménnyj, “variable”), переме́на (pereména, “change”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic неприкосновеньнъ (neprikosnovenĭnŭ). Equivalent to не- (ne-) + прикосну́ться (prikosnútʹsja) + -енный (-ennyj).

parole.significato: there is no, there are no [with genitive ‘something’ and у (u, + genitive) ‘possessed by someone’] (often idiomatically…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic нѣсть (něstĭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic низъити (nizŷiti). By surface analysis, низо- (nizo-) + -йти́ (-jtí).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ниць (nicĭ), from Proto-Slavic *nĩcь.

parole.significato: without a shadow of a doubt; asking no question; nothing wavering (while committing a rash act)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ничто́же сꙋмнѧ́щесѧ (ničtóže sumnę́štesę); an expression used in several New Testament passages, including 1 Cor. 10:25 and 10:27 (corresponding to “asking no question” in King James Version) and James 1:6 (corresponding to “nothing wavering” in King James Version).

parole.significato: night, nighttime (period of time from sundown to sunup)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic нощь (noštĭ) / ⱀⱁⱋⱐ (noštĭ), from Proto-Slavic *noťь. Doublet of ночь (nočʹ), inherited from Old East Slavic.

Inherited from Old East Slavic ноꙗбрь (nojabrĭ), from Old Church Slavonic ноѩбр҄ь (nojębrʹĭ), from Koine Greek Νοέμβριος (Noémbrios). Ultimately from Latin november, from novem, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥ (“nine”) + Latin -ber from -bris, an adjectival suffix.
Inherited from Old East Slavic нравъ (nravŭ), from Old Church Slavonic нравъ (nravŭ), from Proto-Slavic *norvъ. Doublet of но́ров (nórov), from Old East Slavic норовъ (norovŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ноужда (nužda), from Proto-Slavic *nuďa. Displaced the inherited East Slavic form нужа (nuža).

From об- (ob-) + Old Russian and Old Church Slavonic вѣтъ (větŭ, “agreement”), from Proto-Slavic *větъ (“council, talk”). Related words include наве́т (navét), изве́т (izvét), отве́т (otvét), приве́т (privét), сове́т (sovét), ве́че (véče), отвеча́ть (otvečátʹ), отве́тить (otvétitʹ), завеща́ть (zaveš

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обѣтованьнъ (obětovanĭnŭ, “promised”), from Old Church Slavonic обѣтованъ (obětovanŭ, “promised”), which is the past passive participle of Old Church Slavonic обѣтовати (obětovati, “to promise”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обѣщати (oběštati), from Proto-Slavic *oběťati. Displaced native Russian обеча́ть (obečátʹ).

parole.significato: to dwell in, to live in, to inhabit
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обитати (obitati). By surface analysis, об- (ob-) + вита́ть (vitátʹ, “to hover about”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обитѣль (obitělĭ), from Proto-Slavic *obitělь, from *obitati + *-ělь. By surface analysis, обита́ть (obitátʹ, “to inhabit”) + -ель (-elʹ). Cognates include Serbo-Croatian obitelj.

parole.significato: to possess, to have, to own
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обладати (obladati), from Proto-Slavic *obvoldati, imperfective of *obolsti.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic облакъ (oblakŭ), from Proto-Slavic *obolkъ. Displaced native Old East Slavic оболоко (oboloko). By surface analysis, об- (ob-) + во́лок (vólok) + -о (-o) (akin to волочи́ть (voločítʹ), влечь (vlečʹ)).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic область (oblastĭ), from Proto-Slavic *obolstь. Displaced native Old East Slavic оболость (obolostĭ).

parole.significato: to array, to vest, to robe in (to clothe/ornament)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic облачити (oblačiti). By surface analysis, об (ob) + влачи́ть (vlačítʹ). Doublet of обволочи́ть (obvoločítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic облѣщи (oblěšti). By surface analysis, об- (ob-) + влечь (vlečʹ). Doublet of обволо́чь (obvolóčʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обогатити (obogatiti). By surface analysis, о- (o-) + бога́тый (bogátyj) + -и́ть (-ítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обогащати (obogaštati). By surface analysis, обогати́ть (obogatítʹ) + -а́ть (-átʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обратити (obratiti), from Proto-Slavic *obvortiti, a derivative of *vortiti. Doublet of обороти́ть (oborotítʹ), the inherited Old East Slavic form.

parole.significato: to gain, to acquire, to be blessed with
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обрѣсти (obrěsti), from Proto-Slavic *obrěsti. Compare встре́тить (vstrétitʹ).

parole.significato: to gain, to acquire, to be blessed with
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обрѣтати (obrětati), from Proto-Slavic *obrětati. By surface analysis, обрет- (obret-) + -а́ть (-átʹ). Compare встретить (vstretitʹ).
From обрет- (obret-) + -е́ние (-énije) or borrowed directly from Old Church Slavonic обрѣтениѥ (obrětenije).

parole.significato: to seize, to grip, to overcome (especially of feelings)
parole.testo: By surface analysis, *o- + *bujati. If not inherited, then Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обоуꙗти (obujati).

parole.significato: commune, collective society (primitive, often clan-based, society with collective ownership of the means of production)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic обьщина (obĭščina), from Old Church Slavonic обьщина (obĭština), from Proto-Slavic *obьťina. Doublet of обчи́на (občína).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обѩзати (objęzati). By surface analysis, об- (ob-) + вяза́ть (vjazátʹ). Compare typologically Latin obligō (< ligō), whence облига́тный (obligátnyj), облига́ция (obligácija), English oblige.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic овощь (ovoštĭ, “fruit”), from Proto-Slavic *ovoťe. Compare native Ukrainian о́воч (óvoč).
Inherited from Old East Slavic овъ (ovŭ) or borrowed from Old Church Slavonic овъ (ovŭ), both from Proto-Slavic *ovъ (“this”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *awas, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew-o-s.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ограда (ograda), from Proto-Slavic *ogorda.

Inherited from Old East Slavic одѣꙗло (odějalo, “garment, blanket”), from Old Church Slavonic одѣꙗло (odějalo, “outerwear, cloak”), from Old Church Slavonic дѣти (děti, “to set, to place”), from Proto-Slavic *o(b)dějadlo, from *děti (“to do, to place”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-, whence Engli

parole.significato: raiment, attire, garb, habiliments (usually festive, solemn)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic одѣѩиѥ (odějęije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic озарити (ozariti), from Proto-Slavic *ozariti. By surface analysis, о- (o-) + заря́ (zarjá) + -и́ть (-ítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic озарꙗти (ozarjati). By surface analysis, озар- (ozar-) + -я́ть (-játʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic окаꙗньнъ (okajanĭnŭ). By surface analysis, окай- (okaj-) + -анный (-annyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic окрьстъ (okrĭstŭ). By surface analysis, о- (o-) + кре́ст (krést). Compare Bulgarian о́кръст (ókrăst), Polabian vuokárst (“circle”).

parole.significato: ablution (the act of washing or cleansing)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic омъвеньѥ (omŭvenĭje). By surface analysis, омы́ть (omýtʹ) + -ение (-enije). Doublet of омы́тие (omýtije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic омрачати (omračati). By surface analysis, омрачи́ть (omračítʹ) + -а́ть (-átʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic омрачити (omračiti), from Proto-Slavic *obmorčiti. By surface analysis, о- (o-) + мрачи́ть (mračítʹ). Doublet of обморо́чить (obmoróčitʹ).

parole.significato: to determine (to set the limits of)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic опрѣдѣлити (oprěděliti). By surface analysis, о- (o-) + преде́л (predél) + -ить (-itʹ). Compare typologically Latin defīniō (< fīnio < fīnis, note фина́л (finál), фи́ниш (fíniš), дефини́ция (definícija)), Latin determinō (< terminō < terminus, note те́рмин (términ),
Inherited from Old East Slavic орѫдие (orǫdije), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic орѫдиѥ (orǫdije), from Proto-Slavic *orǫdьje.
Inherited from Old East Slavic орѫжие (orǫžije), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic орѫжиѥ (orǫžije), from Proto-Slavic *orǫžьje. Doublet of ружьё (ružʹjó).

parole.significato: to light, to light up, to illuminate
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic освѣтити (osvětiti). By surface analysis, о- (o-) + свет (svet) + -и́ть (-ítʹ).

parole.significato: to light, to light up, to illuminate
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic освѣщати (osvěštati). By surface analysis, освети́ть (osvetítʹ) + -а́ть (-átʹ).

parole.significato: to overhang, to spread (above), to spread as a canopy (over)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic осѣнити (osěniti). By surface analysis, о (o) + сень (senʹ) + -ить (-itʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оскврьнити (oskvrĭniti).

parole.significato: to open (the mouth or face) in a grin
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic склабити сѩ (sklabiti sję, “to smile”), ultimately, from Proto-Slavic *skolbiti. Cognate with Old East Slavic осколобление (oskoloblenije, “smile”), Czech šklebit (“to grin”), ošklíbat sе (“to grin”), Slovak skľabiť sa (“to grin”), Old Polish skɫobiony. Distantly re
The plural of оста́нок (ostánok) (archaic), from Old Church Slavonic останъкъ (ostanŭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ostanъkъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic осѧѕати (osędzati) (1sg. осѧѕаѭ (osędzajǫ) or осѧжѫ (osęžǫ)), variant (showing the Slavic progressive palatalization) of Proto-Slavic *obsęgati.

parole.significato: to avert, to ward off, to prevent
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic отъвратити (otŭvratiti). By surface analysis, от- (ot-) + -врати́ть (-vratítʹ, “to turn”). Doublet of отвороти́ть (otvorotítʹ).

parole.significato: to avert, to ward off, to prevent
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic отъвращати (otŭvraštati). By surface analysis, от (ot) + вращать (vraščatʹ).

parole.significato: revelation (the act of revealing or disclosing)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic отъкръвениѥ (otŭkrŭvenije, “revelation”), from Old Church Slavonic отъкрꙑти (otŭkryti, “to open, reveal”). Related to откры́ть (otkrýtʹ, “to open, reveal”). Doublet of откры́тие (otkrýtije, “opening, discovery, revelation”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic отъкръвеньнъ (otŭkrŭvenĭnŭ, “open”), from отъкръвенъ (otŭkrŭvenŭ, “opened”) + -ьнъ (-ĭnŭ). Doublet of откры́тый (otkrýtyj, “open, sincere”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic отълагати (otŭlagati), from Proto-Slavic *otъlagati. By surface analysis, от- (ot-) + -лага́ть (-lagátʹ). Compare it's neutral counterpart откла́дывать (otkládyvatʹ).

parole.significato: not at all, by no means
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic отънѭдь (otŭnjǫdĭ).

parole.significato: to deny (to assert that something is not true)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic отърицати (otŭricati). Compare the native Russian отрека́ться impf (otrekátʹsja, “disown, disavow; abdicate”).

parole.significato: to feel, to sense, to perceive, to appreciate (to be aware of)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ощоутити (oštutiti), from Proto-Slavic *oťutiti. Doublet of очути́ться (očutítʹsja), the inherited East Slavic form.

parole.significato: to feel, to sense, to perceive, to appreciate (to be aware of)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ощоущати (oštuštati). Doublet of очучать (očučatʹ), the inherited East Slavic form.

parole.significato: great harm, absolute ruin, perdition, destruction; bane
parole.testo: From Old Church Slavonic пагоуба (paguba), from Proto-Slavic *paguba. Compare Bulgarian за́губа (záguba), Polish zguba.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic падежь (padežĭ), from Proto-Slavic *padežь. Doublet of падёж (padjóž), the inherited East Slavic form. The sense of “grammatical case” is a calque of Latin cāsus, which is also derived from the verb for falling, cadō (and is itself a calque from Ancient Greek πτῶσις
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic па́ки (páki); cognate with па́че (páče).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic паче (pače, “more”), comparative of пакы (paky, “again, moreover”), from Proto-Slavic *paky. Compare па́ки (páki).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пькъло (pĭkŭlo), from Proto-Slavic *pьkъlo.
From Old Church Slavonic персъ (persŭ), from Ancient Greek Πέρσης (Pérsēs).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пещера (peštera, “cave”), from Proto-Slavic *peťera, from *peťь (“oven”) + *-era, from *peťi (“to bake”) + *-tь. Doublet of печо́ра (pečóra), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пещь (peštĭ), from Proto-Slavic *peťь. Doublet of печь (pečʹ), the inherited East Slavic form.

parole.significato: drinking, act of drinking (of wine), a drink (verbal noun of пить (pitʹ) (nomen actionis instantiae))
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic питиѥ (pitije). Doublet of питьё (pitʹjó), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пища (pišta), from Proto-Slavic *piťa. By surface analysis, пит(а́ть) (pit(átʹ)) + Proto-Slavic *-ja.

Variant of пла́мя (plámja), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic. Compare Bulgarian пла́мен (plámen), Serbo-Croatian пла̏ме̄н, Slovene plámen (gen. sg. plaména)), Czech plamen, Slovak plameň, Polish płomień.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пламꙑ (plamy, “flame”), from Proto-Slavic *polmy (“flame”). Doublet of по́лымя (pólymja) and по́ломя (pólomja), the inherited East Slavic forms.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пластꙑрь (plastyrĭ), from Vulgar Latin *plastrum.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic платьно (platĭno). Doublet of полотно́ (polotnó), which was inherited.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic плачевьнъ (plačevĭnŭ). By surface analysis, плач (plač) + -ев (-ev) + -ный (-nyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic плѣвелъ (plěvelŭ), from Proto-Slavic *pelvelъ. Displaced половелъ (polovelŭ), the East Slavic form.
Inherited from Old East Slavic плѣнъ (plěnŭ), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic плѣнъ (plěnŭ, “booty”), from Proto-Slavic *pelnъ. Compare the inherited East Slavic doublet поло́н (polón).
Inherited from Old East Slavic побѣда (poběda, “victory, defeat”), from Old Church Slavonic побѣда (poběda, “victory”), from Proto-Slavic *poběda.

parole.significato: to win, to be victorious over, to conquer, to vanquish, to defeat
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic побѣдити (poběditi), from Proto-Slavic *poběditi, from *běditi. Related to the noun беда́ (bedá). Compare Serbo-Croatian побије́дити/pobijéditi, Bulgarian победя́ (pobedjá).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic поборьникъ (poborĭnikŭ), from поборати (poborati, “to help in a struggle, to protect”), from борь (borĭ, “struggle”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic повинѫти сѧ (povinǫti sę), remodeled after class 2 verbs based on present tense forms. Compare Middle Russian повину́ться (povinútʹsja).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic повиновениѥ (povinovenije), from Old Church Slavonic повинѫти сѧ (povinǫti sę). By surface analysis, повинова́ть(ся) (povinovátʹ(sja)) + -е́ние (-énije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic поглътити (poglŭtiti). By surface analysis, по- (po-) + -глоти́ть (-glotítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic поглъщати (poglŭštati). By surface analysis, поглоти́ть (poglotítʹ) + -а́ть (-átʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic подвигъ (podvigŭ), a deverbal of подвигнѫти (podvignǫti). Related to дви́нуть (dvínutʹ) and дви́гать (dvígatʹ).

parole.significato: to rouse, to induce, to encourage
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic подвигнѫти (podvignǫti). Doublet of подвинуть (podvinutʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic подобьѥ (podobĭje), from Proto-Slavic *podobьje, ultimately derived from *doba.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic подобострастенъ (podobostrastenŭ), from подоба (podoba, “manner”) + страстенъ (strastenŭ, “passionate”).

parole.significato: to imitate, to copy, to ape
parole.testo: Probably literally, “to go the same path that someone has gone”, or more loosely translated as “to follow in someone's footsteps”, from Old Church Slavonic дра́га (drága, “road, path, way”) (see доро́га (doróga)). Over time, the meaning shifted to "to reproduce something or someone's actions".
A borrowing from Old Church Slavonic. By surface analysis, по- (po-) + зла́то (zláto) + -и́ть (-ítʹ).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic позорище (pozorište). By surface analysis, позо́р (pozór) + -ище (-išče). (theater): Compare typologically Irish amharclann (< amharc), Ancient Greek θέατρον (théatron) (whence теа́тр (teátr)) (a verbal noun of θεάομαι (theáomai)).
