Inherited from Middle Russian покамѣстъ (pokaměst) (по ка мѣстъ att. since 1560s), from earlier покамѣста (pokaměsta) (по ка мѣста since 1509), presumably from Old Church Slavonic по (po) каꙗ (kaja) мѣста (města) (att. in Middle Russian since 1559), literally 'to which places' or 'until which places
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic покръвител҄ь (pokrŭvitelʹĭ), from покрꙑти (pokryti, “to protect”) + -тел҄ь (-telʹĭ, “-er”). By surface analysis, покров- (pokrov-) + -итель (-itelʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic покоусити сѧ (pokusiti sę, “to attempt”). By surface analysis, по- (po-) + куси́ть (kusítʹ) + -ся (-sja).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic покоушати сѧ (pokušati sę, “to attempt, to try”). By surface analysis, покуси́ться (pokusítʹsja) + -а́ть (-átʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic полагати (polagati), from Proto-Slavic *polagati. By surface analysis, по- (po-) + -лага́ть (-lagátʹ).

parole.significato: to cause to swell, fill with, occupy, enrich
parole.testo: Directly or via Old Church Slavonic from Proto-Slavic *pьlniti. By surface analysis, по́лный (pólnyj, “full”) + -ить (-itʹ). Cognate to Ukrainian по́внити (póvnyty), Belarusian по́ўніць (pównicʹ) and parallel forms in most other Slavic languages.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic польза (polĭza), from Proto-Slavic *polьdza, from *po + *lьga. Doublet of dialectal польга (polʹga). Related to нельзя́ (nelʹzjá), лёгкий (ljóxkij).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic помощь (pomoštĭ), from Proto-Slavic *pomoťь. Doublet of помо́чь (pomóčʹ).

parole.significato: to darken, to cover with gloom
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic помрачити (pomračiti). By surface analysis, по- (po-) + мрачи́ть (mračítʹ). Doublet of поморо́чить (pomoróčitʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пон҄еже (ponʹježe), cognates include Bulgarian поне́же (ponéže).

parole.significato: to encourage, to incentivise, to abet (to support, uphold, or aid)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic поощрити (pooštriti), featuring regressive palatalization across "р" (стр > щр). Another example of palatalization across a liquid is found in the conjugation of слать (slatʹ). Doublet of поостри́ть (poostrítʹ, “to spend some time sharpening, to crack some jokes”),

parole.significato: to encourage, to incentivise, to abet (to support, uphold, or aid)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic поощрꙗти (pooštrjati), featuring regressive palatalization across "р" (стр > щр). Another example of palatalization across a liquid is found in the conjugation of слать (slatʹ). Compare native Russian заостря́ть (zaostrjátʹ, “to sharpen, to emphasize”), which does n
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic попъ (popŭ), from Ancient Greek πάπας (pápas), variant of πάππας (páppas, “daddy, papa”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic *попльзновениѥ (*poplĭznovenije), from Old Church Slavonic попльзнѫти сѧ (poplĭznǫti sę, “to slip, to go wrong”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic попьрати (popĭrati), composed as if from по- (po-) + прать (pratʹ, “to crush, to stomp; to go against, to resist”), from Proto-Slavic *pьrati; cognate with попере́ть (poperétʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic попьрище (popĭrište). Equivalent to попр- (popr-) + -ище (-išče).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic поработити (porabotiti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic порабощати (poraboštati).

parole.significato: to blame, to reproach, to censure
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic порицати (poricati). By surface analysis, по- (po-) + -рица́ть (-ricátʹ). Related to речь (rečʹ), -река́ть (-rekátʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic порокъ (porokŭ), from Proto-Slavic *porokъ. Related to порица́ть (poricátʹ).

parole.significato: a mayor in some East Slavic cities, towns, and oblasts.
parole.testo: Old Church Slavonic посадити (posaditi) + -ник (-nik). Can be analysed as по- (po-) + сади́ть (sadítʹ) + -ник (-nik). Named because originally, the posadniks were appointed by the Prince of Kievan Rus as his governors, but were later elected by veche councils.
PIE word  *swé Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic посѣтити (posětiti), from Proto-Slavic *posětiti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic посѣщати (posěštati).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic почьщивати (počĭštivati).

parole.significato: spelling, orthography (act, practice, ability, or subject of forming words with letters, or of reading the letters of w…
parole.testo: From пра́вый (právyj, “correct”) + -о- (-o-) + писа́ть (pisátʹ, “to write”) + -а́ние (-ánije), or their equivalents in Old Church Slavonic, calque of Ancient Greek ὀρθογραφία (orthographía), from ὀρθός (orthós, “correct”) and γράφω (gráphō, “I write”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic православьнъ (pravoslavĭnŭ), in turn a calque of Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos). By surface analysis, пра́вый (právyj, “right, correct”) + -о- (-o-) + сла́ва (sláva, “glory, glorification; (general) opinion”) + -ный (-nyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic праздьньство (prazdĭnĭstvo). By surface analysis, праздный (prazdnyj) + -ество (-estvo).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic праздьникъ (prazdĭnikŭ, “holiday”), from Proto-Slavic *porzdьnikъ (“skip, gap in a sequence”), derived from *porzdьnъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic праздьновати (prazdĭnovati). By surface analysis, праздный (prazdnyj) + -овать (-ovatʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic праздьнъ (prazdĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *porzdьnъ. Doublet of поро́жний (poróžnij), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прапоръ (praporŭ), from Proto-Slavic *porporъ.
From пра́пор (prápor) + -щик (-ščik), from Old Church Slavonic прапоръ (praporŭ), from Proto-Slavic *porporъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прахъ (praxŭ), from Proto-Slavic *porxъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pers-. Doublet of по́рох (pórox), the inherited East Slavic form.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic праща (prašta), from Proto-Slavic *porťa, from *per- (“to beat”). Displaced Old East Slavic пороча (poroča). Cognate with Polish proca, Bulgarian пра́шка (práška), Slovene prača, Serbo-Croatian пра̏ћа / prȁća. Compare Slovak prak.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пре- (pre-), прѣ- (prě-), from Proto-Slavic *per-. Compare native пере- (pere-).

parole.significato: stay, sojourn (abode, holiday or temporary residence)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣбꙑваниѥ (prěbyvanije). By surface analysis, пребыва́ть (prebyvátʹ) + -а́ние (-ánije).

parole.significato: to be (at some place), to stay, to remain
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣбꙑвати (prěbyvati). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + быва́ть (byvátʹ). Compare Ukrainian перебува́ти (perebuváty).

parole.significato: to be (at some place), to stay, to remain
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣбꙑти (prěbyti). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + быть (bytʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣвъзити (prěvŭziti), remodeled after native взойти́ (vzojtí). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + взойти́ (vzojtí).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣвъзнести (prěvŭznesti). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + вознести́ (voznestí).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣвъзносити (prěvŭznositi). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + возноси́ть (voznosítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣвъсходити (prěvŭsxoditi). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + восходи́ть (vosxodítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣвратити (prěvratiti), from Proto-Slavic *pervortiti. By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + -врати́ть (-vratítʹ, “to turn”). Doublet of перевороти́ть (perevorotítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣвратьнъ (prěvratĭnŭ). Compare also Czech převratný, Polish przewrotny.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣвращати (prěvraštati). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + враща́ть (vraščátʹ, “to turn”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣвꙑше (prěvyše).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣгрѣшениѥ (prěgrěšenije). By surface analysis, прегреши́ть (pregrešítʹ) + -е́ние (-énije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдъ (prědŭ). Doublet of пе́ред (péred), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдъ- (prědŭ-).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдавати (prědavati). Doublet of передава́ть (peredavátʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣданиѥ (prědanije). By surface analysis, предать (predatʹ) + -ание (-anije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдатель (prědatelĭ). By surface analysis, преда́ть (predátʹ, “to betray”) + -тель (-telʹ, “er”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдати (prědati), from Proto-Slavic *perdati, from *per- + *dati. Doublet of переда́ть (peredátʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдъварити (prědŭvariti). Synchoronically analyzable as пред- (pred-) + вари́ть (varítʹ), ultimately, from Proto-Slavic *variti (“to overtake”)
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдъварꙗти (prědŭvarjati). Synchoronically analyzable as пред- (pred-) + вар- (var-) + -ять (-jatʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдѣлъ (prědělŭ). Doublet of переде́л (peredél), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдълагати (prědŭlagati). By surface analysis, пред- (pred-) + -лага́ть (-lagátʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдъложити (prědŭložiti). By surface analysis, пред- (pred-) + ложи́ть (ložítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдъкъ (prědŭkŭ); By surface analysis, пред (pred) + -ок (-ok), from Proto-Slavic *perdъkъ. Doublet of передок (peredok).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдъставити (prědŭstaviti), from прѣдъ- (prědŭ-) + ставити (staviti).

parole.significato: to avert, to stave off, to prevent
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдотъвратити (prědotŭvratiti). By surface analysis, пред- (pred-) + отврати́ть (otvratítʹ).

parole.significato: to avert, to stave off, to prevent
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдотъвращати (prědotŭvraštati). By surface analysis, пред- (pred-) + отвраща́ть (otvraščátʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдъставлꙗти (prědŭstavljati).

parole.significato: to lie ahead, to be at hand, to be in the offing
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдъстоꙗти (prědŭstojati). By surface analysis, пред- (pred-) + стоя́ть (stojátʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдътеча (prědŭteča). By surface analysis, пред- (pred-) + течь (tečʹ) + -а (-a).
From предыдти́ (predydtí, “go past”) + -ущий (-uščij, “(present participle ending)”), from Old Church Slavonic прѣдъити (prědŷiti). See English preterite for a similar semantic development.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣжде (prěžde).

parole.significato: to despise, to hold in contempt
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣзирати (prězirati) (whence also Bulgarian презирам (preziram)). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + -зира́ть (-zirátʹ). See Proto-Slavic *zьrěti for more. Compare typologically Latin dēspiciō (whence English despise) (< dē- + speciō). Also compare ненави́деть (nen

parole.significato: to despise, to hold in contempt
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣзьрѣти (prězĭrěti). Equivalent to пре- (pre-) + зреть (zretʹ).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣкословиѥ (prěkoslovije), from прѣко (prěko, “against”) (compare Serbo-Croatian при̏jеко (“across, through, against”), Russian поперёк (poperjók, “across, crosswise”)) + слово (slovo, “word”) + -иѥ (-ije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣкрасьнъ (prěkrasĭnŭ). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + кра́сный (krásnyj).

parole.significato: to stop, to cease, to end, to discontinue
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣкратити (prěkratiti). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + кра́ткий (krátkij) + -ить (-itʹ).

parole.significato: to stop, to cease, to end, to discontinue
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣкращати (prěkraštati). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + кра́ткий (krátkij) + -ать (-atʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣльсть (prělĭstĭ), from Proto-Slavic *perlьstь (“allure”). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + лесть (lestʹ).

parole.significato: to charm, to tempt, to entice, to seduce, to captivate, to lure, to attract, to dazzle
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣльстити (prělĭstiti). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + льстить (lʹstitʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣмѫдръ (prěmǫdrŭ), also analysed as пре- (pre-) + му́дрый (múdryj). Compare Macedonian пре́мудар (prémudar) and Bulgarian премъ́дър (premắdăr).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пьрѣниѥ (pĭrěnije), from Proto-Slavic *pьrěnьje, from Proto-Slavic *pьrěti. Analysable as прать (pratʹ) + -е́ния (-énija) or пере́ть (perétʹ) + -е́ния (-énija).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣобразити (prěobraziti). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + образи́ть (obrazítʹ).

parole.significato: to transform (into), to turn (into), to reform (into), to reorganize (into, as)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣобразовати (prěobrazovati). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + образова́ть (obrazovátʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣодолѣвати (prěodolěvati). By surface analysis, пре (pre) + одоле- (odole-) + -ва́ть (-vátʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣодолѣти (prěodolěti). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + одоле́ть (odolétʹ).
Probably borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣподобьнъ (prěpodobĭnŭ). Compare Ukrainian преподо́бний (prepodóbnyj), Belarusian прападо́бны (prapadóbny).

parole.significato: a reaching of the midpoint of something; prime, mid-life, etc.
parole.testo: Derived from Old Church Slavonic прѣполовление (prěpolovlenije), from прѣполовити (prěpoloviti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣпона (prěpona), from Proto-Slavic *perpona. Cognate with пина́ть (pinátʹ, “to kick”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣсмꙑкати сѧ (prěsmykati sę, “to creep, to crawl”), from Proto-Slavic *smykati. By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + смыка́ть (smykátʹ) + -ся (-sja).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣстолъ (prěstolŭ), from Proto-Slavic *perstolъ. Note prefixless Polish stolec.

parole.significato: to break, to infringe, to violate (laws, regulations, norms, etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣстѫпати (prěstǫpati), compare native переступа́ть (perestupátʹ). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + ступа́ть (stupátʹ).

parole.significato: to break, to infringe, to violate (laws, regulations, norms, etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣстѫпити (prěstǫpiti), compare native переступи́ть (perestupítʹ). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + ступи́ть (stupítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣстѫплениѥ (prěstǫplenije). By surface analysis, преступи́ть (prestupítʹ) + -е́ние (-énije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣстѫпьникъ (prěstǫpĭnikŭ). By surface analysis, преступи́ть (prestupítʹ) + -ник (-nik).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣтворити (prětvoriti). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + твори́ть (tvorítʹ). Doublet of native dialectal перетвори́ть (peretvorítʹ). Compare Ukrainian перетворити (peretvoryty).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣтварꙗти (prětvarjati). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + тво́р- (tvór-) + -я́ть (-játʹ). Doublet of native dialectal перетворя́ть (peretvorjátʹ).

parole.significato: to suffer, to endure, to go (through)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣтрьпѣти (prětrĭpěti). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + терпе́ть (terpétʹ). Doublet of native перетерпе́ть (pereterpétʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣтити (prětiti, “to threaten”), from Proto-Slavic *pertiti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic привлѣщи (privlěšti). By surface analysis, при- (pri-) + влечь (vlečʹ). Doublet of приволо́чь (privolóčʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic призракъ (prizrakŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прикосновеньѥ (prikosnovenĭje).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прилежьнъ (priležĭnŭ). By surface analysis, (archaic, literary) прилежа́ть (priležátʹ) + -ный (-nyj)
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic приобрѣсти (priobrěsti). By surface analysis, при- (pri-) + обрести́ (obrestí).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic приобрѣтати (priobrětati). By surface analysis, приобрет- (priobret-) + -а́ть (-átʹ).
From приобрет- (priobret-) + -е́ние (-énije) or borrowed directly from Old Church Slavonic приобрѣтениѥ (priobrětenije).

parole.significato: talk of the town (a topic or person discussed by many people)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic притъча въ ѩзꙑцѣхъ (pritŭča vŭ języcěxŭ) "a fable/parable in/among the people", following its semantics and grammar. It's used several times in the Old Testament.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пришьльць (prišĭlĭcĭ), пришельць (prišelĭcĭ). By surface analysis, прише́л (prišél) + -ец (-ec).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пришьствиѥ (prišĭstvije), пришествиѥ (prišestvije). By surface analysis, прише́д (prišéd) + -ствие (-stvije).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic приѩтьнъ (prijętĭnŭ, “acceptable, pleasant”), from Old Church Slavonic приѩтъ (prijętŭ, “received, accepted”) + -ьнъ (-ĭnŭ). Equivalent to прия́т(ый) (priját(yj)) + -ный (-nyj). Compare Ukrainian прийня́тний (pryjnjátnyj, “acceptable”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прозѧбати (prozębati), from Proto-Slavic *zębnǫti (“to germinate”). Unrelated to зя́бнуть (zjábnutʹ, “to freeze”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic произволъ (proizvolŭ). Can also be analysed as про- (pro-) + из- (iz-) + во́ля (vólja)
Inherited from Old East Slavic проказа (prokaza, “leprosy”), from Old Church Slavonic проказа (prokaza, “leprosy”), from Proto-Slavic *prokaza.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic проницати (pronicati), from Proto-Slavic *nicati (“to arise”). Related to проника́ть (pronikátʹ).
Most likely borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пронꙑръ (pronyrŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic проповѣдьникъ (propovědĭnikŭ, “herald, messenger”). By surface analysis, пропове́дать (propovédatʹ) + -ник (-nik).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic проповѣдь (propovědĭ) or пропове́дать (propovédatʹ) + -ь (-ʹ), from Proto-Slavic *propovědь.

From Old Church Slavonic простълюдинъ (prostŭljudinŭ), from про́стъ (próstŭ, “simple, ordinary”) and людинъ (ljudinŭ, “free man”); see просто́й (prostój) and лю́ди (ljúdi). Compare with Ukrainian просто́люд (prostóljud, “commoners (collective)”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пространьство (prostranĭstvo), from Proto-Slavic *prostornьstvo. By surface analysis, про- (pro-) + страна́ (straná, “country, region”) + -ство (-stvo).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic псалъмъ (psalŭmŭ), from Ancient Greek ψαλμός (psalmós). Doublet of пса́льма (psálʹma).
From Old East Slavic псалътꙑрь (psalŭtyrĭ), from Old Church Slavonic псалътꙑр҄ь (psalŭtyrʹĭ), from Ancient Greek ψαλτήριον (psaltḗrion).
From Old East Slavic псалътꙑрь (psalŭtyrĭ), from Old Church Slavonic псалътꙑр҄ь (psalŭtyrʹĭ), from Ancient Greek ψαλτήριον (psaltḗrion).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic поукъ (pukŭ), from Proto-Slavic *pǫkъ, from Proto-Indo-European *pank-. Compare Ukrainian пук (puk), Czech puk, Polish pęk. Further cognates, per Vasmer, are Persian پنگ (pang, “date palm cluster”) and Latin pānus (“millet ear”).

parole.significato: slave, serf, bondslave (in common sense and about male person, not female separately)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рабъ (rabŭ) via Old East Slavic рабъ (rabŭ), from Proto-Slavic *orbъ. Displaced Old East Slavic робъ (robŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic равьнъ (ravĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *orvьnъ. Doublet of ро́вный (róvnyj), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic разбои (razboi), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *orzbojь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic развѣ (razvě, “only, besides”), from Proto-Slavic *orzvě. Displaced Old East Slavic розвѣ (rozvě)
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic раздоръ (razdorŭ), from Proto-Slavic *orzdorъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic различьнъ (različĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *orzličьnъ. By surface analysis, раз- (raz-) + ли́чный (líčnyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic разьнъ (razĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *orzьnъ. Doublet of ро́зный (róznyj). See also рознь (roznʹ), раз (raz), ре́зать (rézatʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic разоумъ (razumŭ), from Proto-Slavic *orzumъ. Displaced native *розум (*rozum).

parole.significato: to understand (to be aware of the meaning of)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic разумѣти (razuměti), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic разоумѣти (razuměti), from Proto-Slavic *orzuměti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic распьрꙗ (raspĭrja), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *pьrěti (“to quarrel”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рьвьньѥ, рьвениѥ (rĭvĭnĭje, rĭvenije), from *рьвьнь (*rĭvĭnĭ, “zeal”) + -ьѥ (-ĭje). Cognate with Russian ре́вность (révnostʹ)
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic раждати (raždati), from Proto-Slavic *raďati. Doublet of рожа́ть (rožátʹ), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ръпътати (rŭpŭtati), from Proto-Slavic *rъpъtati.

parole.significato: boundary, border, borderline, frontier (the line or frontier area separating regions)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рубежь (rubežĭ), from Proto-Slavic *rǫbežь, from *rǫbiti (“to chop, hem”) + *-ežь. Doublet of рубёж (rubjóž).

From Old Church Slavonic рьдьръ (rĭdĭrŭ) (Russian), via vowel assimilation from *ръдьръ (*rŭdĭrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rъdrъ; cognate with Old East Slavic ръдръ (rŭdrŭ). рьдьръ (rĭdĭrŭ) + -ый (-yj) developed to *ре́дрый (*rédryj), then to the modern form рёдрый (rjódryj) by diphthongization (see Hist

From Old Church Slavonic санъ (sanŭ) (u-stem), probably of Oghur origin. Cognate with Turkish san (“reputation”), Turkmen san (“account”), Kazakh санау (sanaw, “count”), Tatar san (“number”) and akin to dial. Inherited from Old East Slavic свѣдѣниѥ (svěděnije), from Old Church Slavonic съвѣдѣниѥ (sŭvěděnije)

parole.significato: eyewitness, witness (one who has a personal knowledge of something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съвѣдѣтель (sŭvědětelĭ). Originally contained the archaic root вѣд- (věd-, “to know”); after regular dissimilation ѣ-ѣ > и-ѣ reanalysed as containing the root вид- (vid-, “to see”), and equivalent to с- (s-) + ви́деть (vídetʹ) + -тель (-telʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съвѣдѣтельство (sŭvědětelĭstvo). By surface analysis, свиде́тель (svidételʹ) + -ство (-stvo).

parole.significato: to testify, to witness, to be evidence (of)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съвѣдѣтельствовати (sŭvědětelĭstvovati). By surface analysis, свиде́тельство (svidételʹstvo) + -овать (-ovatʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic своиствьнъ (svoistvĭnŭ). By surface analysis, сво́йство (svójstvo) + -енный (-ennyj).

parole.significato: property, virtue, quality (attribute or abstract quality associated with an object)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic своиство (svoistvo), which is a calque of Ancient Greek ἰδίωμα (idíōma). By surface analysis, свой (svoj) + -ство (-stvo).

Inherited from Old East Slavic свꙗтокъ (svjatokŭ) from Old Church Slavonic свѧтъкъ (svętŭkŭ), from Old Church Slavonic свѧтъ (svętŭ) (< Proto-Slavic *svętъ) + Old Church Slavonic -ъкъ (-ŭkŭ) (< Proto-Slavic *-ъkъ). Compare Carpathian Rusyn святкы (svjatkŷ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic свѧщеньнъ (svęštenĭnŭ). By surface analysis, святи́ть (svjatítʹ) + -енный (-ennyj). Doublet of свячёный (svjačónyj).
Perhaps borrowed from Old Church Slavonic себѣ (sebě) or inherited from Old East Slavic собѣ (sobě); both from Proto-Slavic *sebě.

Inherited from Old East Slavic седмъ (sedmŭ), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic седмъ (sedmŭ), compared dialectal сёмый (sjómyj). From Proto-Slavic *sedmъ (“seventh”), from earlier *sebdmъ < *septmъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *septmas, from Proto-Indo-European *septmós.

PIE word  *septḿ̥ Inherited from Old East Slavic сентѧбрь (sentębrĭ), семтѧбрь (semtębrĭ), септѧбрь (septębrĭ), септѧбръ (septębrŭ), септѧмбрь (septęmbrĭ), via Old Church Slavonic септѧбр҄ь (septębrʹĭ), from Byzantine Greek Σεπτέμβριος (Septémbrios) from Latin september (“seventh month”), from septe
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сѣтовати (sětovati), from Proto-Slavic *sětovati. Cognate with Serbo-Croatian се̏та.
From Old Church Slavonic сѵнаго́га (sünagóga), from Ancient Greek σῠνᾰγωγή (sŭnăgōgḗ, “assembly, gathering”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сионовъ (sionovŭ). By surface analysis, Сио́н (Sión) + -овый (-ovyj). Compare Ukrainian сіо́новий (siónovyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скврьна (skvrĭna), from Proto-Slavic *skvьrna. The inherited form would be *сквёрна (*skvjórna). Related to Czech skvrna, Slovak škvrna.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скврьнословиѥ (skvrĭnoslovije). By surface analysis, скве́рный (skvérnyj) + -о- (-o-) + сло́во (slóvo) + -ие (-ije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скврьнъ (skvrĭnŭ). By surface analysis, скве́рна (skvérna) + -ный (-nyj).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скꙑтати сѧ (skytati sę), from Proto-Slavic *skytati (sę). Cognate with Ukrainian скита́тися (skytátysja), Bulgarian ски́там се (skítam se), Serbo-Croatian скитати, Slovene skítati sе. More distantly cognate with Lithuanian kutė́ti (“to shake”), Proto-Germanic *skund
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скрьжьтати (skrĭžĭtati), from Proto-Slavic *skrьgъtati.

parole.significato: table, tablet (with sacred text inscribed upon it)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic скрижаль (skrižalĭ), which is possibly borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скрижаль (skrižalĭ), ultimately, from Proto-Slavic *skrižalь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сълагати (sŭlagati). By surface analysis, с- (s-) + -лага́ть (-lagátʹ). Compare it's neutral counterpart скла́дывать (skládyvatʹ).
PIE word  *sḗh₂l Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сладъкъ (sladŭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *soldъkъ. See also the dialectal Russian соло́дкий (solódkij), a doublet.
Plural of сласть (slastʹ), from Old Church Slavonic сласть (slastĭ, “pleasure, sweetness”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сласть (slastĭ), from Proto-Slavic *solstь. The native Old East Slavic *солость (*solostĭ) is unattested, but is the source of солости́ть (solostítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic словесьнъ (slovesĭnŭ).
From Old Church Slavonic слоужитель (služitelĭ). By surface analysis, служи́ть (služítʹ) + -тель (-telʹ)

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic смръдъ (smrŭdŭ, “someone who stinks”), related to смерде́ть (smerdétʹ, “to stink”). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *smьrdъ, Proto-Slavic *smьrdě̀ti (“to stink”) Cognates include Ukrainian смерд (smerd), Belarusian смерд (smjerd) or Belarusian смердзь (smjerdzʹ), Polis
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic змѵ́рьна (zmǘrĭna), from Ancient Greek σμύρνα (smúrna).
Derived from Old Church Slavonic смрадъ (smradŭ), from Proto-Slavic *smȏrdъ. Displaced the native East Slavic form смо́род (smórod) from Old East Slavic смородъ (smorodŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съмѫтити (sŭmǫtiti).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съмѫщениѥ (sŭmǫštenije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сънѣдь (sŭnědĭ).

parole.significato: to get, to win, to gain
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сънискати (sŭniskati). Compare native сыскать (syskatʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съ- (sŭ-), from Proto-Slavic *sъ(n)-; see above.

parole.significato: speaking partner, other person (with whom one is talking), interlocutor
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic събесѣдьникъ (sŭbesědĭnikŭ). By surface analysis, со- (so-) + бесе́да (beséda) + -ник (-nik).

parole.significato: interview (a formal meeting for the assessment of a candidate or applicant)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic събесѣдованиѥ (sŭbesědovanije). By surface analysis, собесе́довать (sobesédovatʹ) + -ние (-nije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съблазнъ (sŭblaznŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sъblaznъ, from *blaznь.

parole.significato: to comply, to obey, to observe, to follow, to stick (to)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съблюдати (sŭbljudati), from Proto-Slavic *sъbľudati. By surface analysis, соблюд- (sobljud-) + -а́ть (-átʹ).

parole.significato: to comply, to obey, to observe, to follow, to stick (to)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съблюсти (sŭbljusti). Equivalent со- (so-) + блюсти́ (bljustí).

parole.significato: cathedral, catholicon (a large church, usually the current or former seat of a bishop)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съборъ (sŭborŭ) (a calque of Ancient Greek συναγωγή (sunagōgḗ)), from Proto-Slavic *sъborъ. Doublet of сбор (sbor), the inherited East Slavic form.

parole.significato: to accomplish, to perform, to commit, to perpetrate, to make
parole.testo: From Old Church Slavonic съврьшити (sŭvrĭšiti), from съ- (sŭ-) + връшити (vrŭšiti) from Proto-Indo-European *wers-. Also related to верх (verx, “top, summit”) and to Old East Slavic вьрхъ (vĭrxŭ), Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ. Literally, “to top out”.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съвѣсть (sŭvěstĭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съвѣтъ (sŭvětŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sъvětъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съвратити (sŭvratiti). By surface analysis, со- (so-) + -врати́ть (-vratítʹ, “to turn”). Doublet of свороти́ть (svorotítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съвращати (sŭvraštati). By surface analysis, со- (so-) + враща́ть (vraščátʹ, “to turn”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съглѧдатаи (sŭględatai). By surface analysis, со- (so-) + гляде́ть (gljadétʹ) + -а́тай (-átaj).

parole.significato: to abet (to support, uphold, or aid)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съдѣиствовати (sŭděistvovati). By surface analysis, соде́йство (sodéjstvo) + -овать (-ovatʹ).

parole.significato: to make, to create, to produce, to execute
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съдѣꙗти (sŭdějati). Equivalent to со- (so-) + де́ять (déjatʹ).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съзьдати (sŭzĭdati, “to build, to erect”), from Proto-Slavic *sъzьdati, from *zьdati. The modern conjugation is analogical after дать (datʹ), replacing the old present stem созижд-.

parole.significato: to examine, to see, to behold, to observe, to gaze at
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съзрьцати (sŭzrĭcati), from Proto-Slavic *zьrcati. Related to зреть (zretʹ), -зирать (-ziratʹ). Compare other verbs from the same root зе́риться (zéritʹsja), поза́рится (pozáritsja), зы́ркать (zýrkatʹ), зы́рить (zýritʹ). Compare native dialectal зе́ркать (zérkatʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съзидати (sŭzidati). By surface analysis, со- (so-) + -зида́ть (-zidátʹ).

parole.significato: to shorten, to curtail, to abridge, to abbreviate
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съкратити (sŭkratiti). By surface analysis, со- (so-) + кра́ткий (krátkij) + -ить (-itʹ). Compare the Belarusian скараці́ць (skaracícʹ) and Ukrainian скороти́ти (skorotýty).

parole.significato: to shorten, to curtail, to abridge, to abbreviate
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съкращати (sŭkraštati). By surface analysis, со- (so-) + кра́ткий (krátkij) + -ать (-atʹ).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съкръвеньнъ (sŭkrŭvenĭnŭ, “hidden, concealed”), from съкръвенъ (sŭkrŭvenŭ, “hidden, concealed”) + -ьнъ (-ĭnŭ). Related to сокры́ть (sokrýtʹ) and скры́ть (skrýtʹ). Doublet of скры́тый (skrýtyj, “hidden, concealed”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съкровище (sŭkrovište). By surface analysis, сокры́ть (sokrýtʹ, “to hide, cover”) + -ище (-išče). Compare typologically Proto-Germanic *huzdą (whence English hoard) < Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH-.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съкроушати (sŭkrušati). Equivalent to сокруш- (sokruš-) + -а́ть (-átʹ)
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съкроушити (sŭkrušiti). Equivalent to со- (so-) + круши́ть (krušítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съньмъ (sŭnĭmŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sъnьmъ. Identical to съём (sʺjom), сойм (sojm), суём (sujóm) and сейм (sejm).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съсловие (sŭslovije), from Proto-Slavic *sъslovьje, itself a calque of Ancient Greek σύγκλητος (súnklētos) / σύλλογος (súllogos). By surface analysis, со- (so-) + сло́во (slóvo) + -ие (-ije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съставъ (sŭstavŭ), which itself is a calque of Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma), from σῠν- (sŭn-, with, together) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).

parole.significato: to compete, to vie, to contend
parole.testo: Ultimately from Old Church Slavonic сътѧѕати сѧ (sŭtędzati sę), сътѧзати сѧ (sŭtęzati sę), from Proto-Slavic *tędzati, featuring 3rd palatalization. Compare native тяга́ться (tjagátʹsja), from Proto-Slavic *tęgati without 3rd palatalization.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сътворити (sŭtvoriti). By surface analysis, со- (so-) + твори́ть (tvorítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сътрѧсати (sŭtręsati). By surface analysis, сотрясти́ (sotrjastí) + -а́ть (-átʹ). Doublet of стряса́ть (strjasátʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сътрѧсти (sŭtręsti). By surface analysis, со- (so-) + трясти́ (trjastí). Doublet of стрясти́ (strjastí).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съчетати (sŭčetati). Equivalent to со- (so-) + чета́ (četá) + -ать (-atʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съшьствиѥ (sŭšĭstvije), съшествиѥ (sŭšestvije). By surface analysis, соше́д (sošéd) + -ствие (-stvije).

parole.significato: savior (a person who rescues another from harm)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съпаситель (sŭpasitelĭ). By surface analysis, спас- (spas-) + -тель (-telʹ)
Inherited from Old East Slavic съпасти (sŭpasti), which is a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic съпасти (sŭpasti). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *sъ(n) + *pasti (“to pasture, herd”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic спѫдъ (spǫdŭ, “modius, bushel; vessel of this size”), Russian Church Slavonic спꙋдъ (spudŭ); compare Slovene spọ̑d (“bucket”) (tonal orthography), Old Polish spąd (“bucket”), from Proto-Slavic [Term?]. More distantly cognate with (and per Trubachev, borrowed from) M
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic срамъ (sramŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sormъ. Doublet of соро́м (soróm), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic срачица (sračica). Related to соро́чка (soróčka). Doublet of сорочи́ца (soročíca).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сьребро (sĭrebro), from Proto-Slavic *sьrebro. Doublet of серебро́ (serebró, “silver”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic срѣда (srěda), from Proto-Slavic *serda. Displaced native Old East Slavic середа (sereda, “middle; Wednesday”) (cf. середа́ (seredá)), третииникъ (tretiinikŭ, “Wednesday”, literally “third (day)”).
Apparently, a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic [Term?], from Proto-Slavic *serdina; a doublet of inherited середи́на (seredína).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic срѣдьнъ (srědĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *serdьnъ. Doublet of сере́дний (serédnij), the inherited East Slavic form. By surface analysis, среда́ (sredá) + -ний (-nij).
From the Old East Slavic стихъ (stixŭ), from the Old Church Slavonic стихъ (stixŭ), from the Ancient Greek στίχος (stíkhos, “row, line, verse”).

parole.significato: element (one of the four classical elements of Ancient Greek philosophy)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic стихия (stixija), from Old Church Slavonic стѵхии (stüxii) (feminine form стѵхиꙗ (stüxija)), from Ancient Greek στοιχεῖον (stoikheîon). Compare Ukrainian стихі́я (styxíja), Belarusian стыхі́я (styxíja).

Inherited from Old East Slavic стлъпотвореніє (stlŭpotvorenije, “tower building”) (in the context of Tower of Babel), from Old Church Slavonic стлъпотворѥниѥ (stlŭpotvorjenije), calque of Ancient Greek πυργοποιΐα (purgopoiḯa).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стражь (stražĭ), from Proto-Slavic *storžь (“guard”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *storʔg-. Doublet of сто́рож (stórož).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стража (straža), from Proto-Slavic *storža, from Proto-Slavic *storgja.

Inherited from Old East Slavic страна (strana), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic страна (strana), from Proto-Slavic *storna. Compare the regular East-Slavic reflex with pleophony сторона́ (storoná). Compare typologically English country (<< Latin contrā). Also compare окра́ина (okráina), край (kraj

parole.significato: wanderer, traveller; vagrant, vagabond, rover, roamer, pilgrim
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic страньникъ (stranĭnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *stornьnikъ. By surface analysis, страна́ (straná) + -ник (-nik). Compare Old East Slavic стороньникъ (storonĭnikŭ). Formally, a doublet of сторо́нник (storónnik).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic страньнъ (stranĭnŭ, “fellow countryman, compatriot, strange”). Derived from Old Church Slavonic страна (strana, “country”) (whence Russian страна́ (straná)). parole.significato: the week just before Easter (used only in the terms below)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic страстьнъ (strastĭnŭ).

From Old Church Slavonic стрьмоглавъ (strĭmoglavŭ, “with the head down”) via Russian Church Slavonic forms стрьмъглавъ, стремоглавъ, стремглавъ, which acquired modern meaning in 15th century, from Proto-Slavic *strьmъ + *golva + *-ь. Inherited from Old East Slavic строити (stroiti), from Proto-Slavic *strojiti, from *strojь.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стръпътивъ (strŭpŭtivŭ), from Proto-Slavic *strъpъtivъ.
Denominal of Old Church Slavonic студъ (studŭ, “cool, chill”), from Proto-Slavic *studiti. Compare Proto-Slavic *studenъ.

From Old Church Slavonic студъ (studŭ, “cold”), from Proto-Slavic *studenъ (“cold”), from *studъ (“cold, shame”) and thus cognate with стыд (styd, “shame”). Compare Polish ostuda, Bulgarian студ (stud). Vasmer links the PIE root with Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewd- which, that being true, would expand
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сѫдилище (sǫdilište). By surface analysis, суди́ть (sudítʹ, “to judge”) + -лище (-lišče).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic соуѥ- (suje-), calque of Ancient Greek ματαιο- (mataio-). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *sujь (“futile”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic соуѥвѣрьѥ (sujevěrĭje). By surface analysis, суе- (suje-) + ве́ра (véra) + -ие (-ije).

parole.significato: idle claim/talk/promise (claim, talk, promise without content), verbiage
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic соуѥсловьѥ (sujeslovĭje), calque of Ancient Greek ματαιολογία (mataiología). Equivalent to суе- (suje-, “futile”) + сло́во (slóvo, “word, speech”) + -ие (-ije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic соуѥта (sujeta), from Proto-Slavic *sujeta, from *sujь + *-eta.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сѫмракъ (sǫmrakŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sǫmorkъ. Displaced native Old East Slavic суморокъ (sumorokŭ).
Inherited from Old East Slavic сусѣкъ (susěkŭ) or borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сѫсѣкъ (sǫsěkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sǫsěkъ, related to *sěťi (“to cut”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic сусѣкъ (susěkŭ) or borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сѫсѣкъ (sǫsěkŭ), related to Proto-Slavic *sěťi.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сѫщьство (sǫštĭstvo). By surface analysis, су́щий (súščij) + -ество (-estvo).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сꙑ (sy), present active participle of бꙑти (byti), from Proto-Slavic *sy, present active participle of *byti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic таиньство (tainĭstvo), from Proto-Slavic *tajьnьstvo.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тать (tatĭ), from Proto-Slavic *tatь (“thief”).

parole.significato: the body of a fat person
parole.testo: From the Old Church Slavonic plural of тѣло (tělo).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тѣлесьнъ (tělesĭnŭ), from тѣло (tělo), an s-stem. By surface analysis, телеса́ (telesá) + -ный (-nyj).

Inherited from Old East Slavic темьанъ (temĭanŭ), from Old Church Slavonic темьꙗнъ (temĭjanŭ), from Ancient Greek θῡμίαμα (thūmíama, “incense for smoking”), from θῡμιάω (thūmiáō, “to burn incense, to burn, to smoke (something)”), ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós (“smoke”) (cogna

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тождьство (toždĭstvo). Calque of Latin identitās (literally “sameness”), from Church Slavonic тожде (tožde), from Old Church Slavonic тъжде (tŭžde, “the same”). Compare Russian то́же (tóže), -ество (-estvo).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тръжьство (trŭžĭstvo), from тръгъ (trŭgŭ) + -ьство (-ĭstvo). By surface analysis, торг (torg) + -ество (-estvo).

parole.significato: rite, ceremony (an irregular church ceremony performed at the request of a parishioner)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѣба (trěba), from Proto-Slavic *terba. Displaced the Old East Slavic inherited form тереба (tereba).
Inherited from Old East Slavic трѣбовати (trěbovati), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѣбовати (trěbovati), from Proto-Slavic *terbovati (see *terba).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трьволнъниѥ (trĭvolnŭnije), composed of трь- (trĭ-, “three”) + влъна (vlŭna, “wave”). A calque of Ancient Greek τρι-κυμία (tri-kumía, literally “third wave”), from the belief that the third wave is the most dangerous one (compare девя́тый вал (devjátyj val)).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѣзвъ (trězvŭ), from Proto-Slavic *terzvъ. Doublet of тверёзый (tverjózyj), the inherited East Slavic form.

parole.significato: to tremble, to quiver, to flicker
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трепетати (trepetati), from Proto-Slavic *trepetati.
Compound formed from Old Church Slavonic тоуне (tune) 'given freely; for no purpose' (also found in the adverb вту́не (vtúne)), and *я́дец (*jádec), 'eater' (related to еда́ (jedá, “food”)).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тщедушнъ (tštedušnŭ), a compound of тъщь (tŭštĭ) (compare то́щий (tóščij)) and душа (duša) (compare душа́ (dušá)).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тъщеславьѥ (tŭšteslavĭje, “vainglory”), itself a calque of Ancient Greek κενοδοξία (kenodoxía, “vainglory”). By surface analysis, тще- (tšče-) + слава (slava) + -ие (-ije).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тъщета (tŭšteta), from Proto-Slavic *tъščeta, a derivative of *tъščь (whence то́щий (tóščij)) + *-ota. Further back, from Proto-Indo-European *tweskʷ- (“desert, barren”). Compare Sanskrit तुच्छ (tuccha, “empty, vain”), Latin tesqua (“desert”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тъщетьнъ (tŭštetĭnŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тѧгота (tęgota). Related to тя́жкий (tjážkij).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оубѣдити (uběditi). Proto-Slavic *uběditi, from *běditi. Compare typologically Latin convincō (whence English convince) < vincō (akin to victor) (whence English vanquish).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оубииц (ubiic), from Proto-Slavic *ubьjьcь. By surface analysis, уби́ть (ubítʹ) + -ец (-ec). Compare Russian уби́вец (ubívec) and Ukrainian вби́вець (vbývecʹ).

parole.significato: murder, homicide (the action of killing someone)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оубииство (ubiistvo), from Proto-Slavic *ubьjьstvo. In case of native origin *убе́йство (*ubéjstvo) would be expected, compare семе́йство (seméjstvo) and суде́йство (sudéjstvo). By surface analysis, уби́ть (ubítʹ) + -ство (-stvo). Also compare Russian уби́вство (ubí

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оубиица (ubiica), from Proto-Slavic *ubьjьca. In case of native origin *убе́йца (*ubéjca) would be expected. By surface analysis, уби́ть (ubítʹ) + -ца (-ca). Compare Russian уби́вец (ubívec), уби́вца (ubívca) (dialectal) and Ukrainian уби́вця (ubývcja).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оубити (ubiti), from Proto-Slavic *ubiti. By surface analysis, у- (u-) + бить (bitʹ). Compare Ukrainian уби́ти (ubýty), Serbo-Croatian ùbiti, Slovene ubíti.

parole.significato: to indulge, to humour, to please, to gratify, to pamper
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оублажати (ublažati). By surface analysis, у- (u-) + бла́го (blágo) + -а́ть (-átʹ).

parole.significato: to indulge, to humour, to please, to gratify, to pamper
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оублажити (ublažiti). By surface analysis, у- (u-) + бла́го (blágo) + -ить (-itʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оудавлѥнина /ⱆⰴⰰⰲⰾⰵⱀⰻⱀⰰ (udavljenina).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic удоволити (udovoliti), from Proto-Slavic *udovoliti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оукротити (ukrotiti), from Proto-Slavic *krotiti. By surface analysis, у- (u-) + кро́т(кий) (krót(kij)) + -и́ть (-ítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оумрьтвити (umrĭtviti). By surface analysis, у- (u-) + мёртвый (mjórtvyj) + -и́ть (-ítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оумрьщвлѣти (umrĭštvlěti). By surface analysis, у- (u-) + мёртвый (mjórtvyj) + -я́ть (-játʹ).

parole.significato: to hope (for), to set one's hopes (upon)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оупъвати (upŭvati), from Proto-Slavic *upъvati.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оупраздьнити (uprazdĭniti). By surface analysis, у- (u-) + пра́здный (prázdnyj) + -ить (-itʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оусрьдьѥ (usrĭdĭje). By surface analysis, у- (u-) + се́рдце (sérdce) + -ие (-ije).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оусрьдьнъ (usrĭdĭnŭ). By surface analysis, усе́рдие (usérdije) + -ный (-nyj)
Formed after the past stem of Old East Slavic усънути (usŭnuti) and Old Church Slavonic усънѫти (usŭnǫti), усъп-, further derived from Proto-Slavic *usъnǫti (“to fall asleep”)
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оустранити (ustraniti). By surface analysis, у- (u-) + страна́ (straná) + -и́ть (-ítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оустранꙗти (ustranjati). By surface analysis, устрани́ть (ustranítʹ) + -я́ть (-játʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оухыщрениѥ (uxyštrenije), from оухытрити (uxytriti, “to come up with, to figure out, to do”), from Proto-Slavic *xytrъ (“sly, wise”). Compare хи́трый (xítryj).

Inherited from Old East Slavic участие (učastije), from Old Church Slavonic оучѧстиѥ (učęstije). By surface analysis, участь (učastʹ) + -ие (-ije). The modern meanings arose due to French influence, compare French avoir part and French prendre part, which were calqued as принима́ть уча́стие (prinimá

From Old East Slavic феврарь (fevrarĭ), феуларь (feularĭ), from Old Church Slavonic февроуари (fevruari), from Byzantine Greek Φεβρουάριος (Phebrouários), from Latin Februārius, from Latin februa, from Latin febris (whence also English fever). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰ- (“to burn;
From Old Church Slavonic философъ (filosofŭ), from Ancient Greek φιλόσοφος (philósophos).

parole.significato: the name of the letter Х, х
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic хѣръ (xěrŭ), of uncertain origin: Possibilities include: * Alternative spelling of Old Church Slavonic сѣръ (sěrŭ, “gray”) * An abbreviation of Old Church Slavonic хероувимъ (xeruvimŭ, “cherubim”), from Ancient Greek χερουβίμ (kheroubím), from Hebrew כְּרוּבִים (kər
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic хꙑщьникъ (xyštĭnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xyťьnikъ. By surface analysis, хищ- (xišč-) + -ник (-nik).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic хꙑщьнъ (xyštĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xyťьnъ. By surface analysis, хитить (xititʹ, “to plunder, to reave”) + -ный (-nyj)
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic хладъ (xladŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xoldъ. Doublet of хо́лод (xólod), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic хладьнъ (xladĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xoldьnъ. Doublet of холо́дный (xolódnyj). By surface analysis, хлад (xlad) + -ный (-nyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ходатаи (xodatai). By surface analysis, ходи́ть (xodítʹ) + -а́тай (-átaj).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic храбрость (xrabrostĭ), from Proto-Slavic *xorbrostь. Displaced the native East Slavic form хоробрость (xorobrostʹ). By surface analysis, хра́брый (xrábryj) + -ость (-ostʹ).

parole.significato: brave, courageous (strong in the face of fear)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic храбръ (xrabrŭ, “brave”), from Proto-Slavic *xorbrъ (“brave”). Displaced the native East Slavic form хоро́брый (xoróbryj, “brave”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic храмъ (xramŭ) via Old East Slavic храмъ (xramŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xormъ. Doublet of хоро́мы (xorómy) from хоромъ (xoromŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic хранитель (xranitelĭ). By surface analysis, храни́ть (xranítʹ, “to keep, to guard”) + -тель (-telʹ, “er”).

parole.significato: to keep (to maintain possession of), to preserve, to store
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic хранити (xraniti), from Proto-Slavic *xorniti. Doublet of хорони́ть (xoronítʹ) (see there for more).
Unadapted borrowing from Old Church Slavonic Христосъ въскрьсе (Xristosŭ vŭskrĭse): Literally, “Christ is risen”, a calque of Greek Χριστός ανέστη (Christós anésti), as a Paschal greeting.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic хѫдожьство (xǫdožĭstvo). Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *handuz.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic цѣльбьнъ (cělĭbĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *cělьbьnъ. By surface analysis, (archaic) цельба́ (celʹbá) + -ный (-nyj).

parole.significato: chastity (abstaining from sexual intercourse outside of marriage)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic цѣломѫдриѥ (cělomǫdrije). By surface analysis, це́лый (célyj, “whole”) + -о- (-o-) + му́дрый (múdryj, “wise”) + -ие (-ije).

Inherited from Old East Slavic чьрноризьць (čĭrnorizĭcĭ), from Old Church Slavonic чрьноризьць (črĭnorizĭcĭ); by surface analysis, чёрный (čórnyj, “black”) + -о- (-o-) + ри́за (ríza, “robe, vestment”) + -ец (-ec).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic чрътогъ (črŭtogŭ), compare Ukrainian черто́г (čertóh), Old Serbian чртог, чртаг. Per Vasmer, probably borrowed from Persian چارتاق (čârtâq, “four-arch”). See черда́к (čerdák, “attic”), another borrowing of the same term, for more information.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic *члѣнъ (*člěnŭ), replacing the East Slavic form челен. Both forms stem from Proto-Slavic *čelnъ and are related to колено. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- or *(s)kel- + *-nъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic чрѣво (črěvo), from Proto-Slavic *červo. Doublet of черёво (čerjóvo), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic чрѣда (črěda), from Proto-Slavic *čerda (“file, herd”). Doublet of череда́ (čeredá), the inherited East Slavic form.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic чрѣсъ (črěsŭ) / ⱍⱃⱑⱄⱏ (črěsŭ), from Proto-Slavic *čersъ, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kert-, from *(s)ker-. Doublet of че́рез (čérez), inherited from Old East Slavic.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic чрѣсла (črěsla), from Proto-Slavic *čerslo. Displaced the native East Slavic form че́ресла (čéresla).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic чоувьство (čuvĭstvo), from Proto-Slavic *čuvьstvo, from *čuti (“to sense, feel, notice”) + *-ьstvo. Cognate to чу́ять (čújatʹ), чутьё (čutʹjó).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic чоувьствовати (čuvĭstvovati). By surface analysis, чу́вство (čúvstvo) + -овать (-ovatʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic щоуждь (štuždĭ), from Proto-Slavic *ťuďь. Doublet of чужо́й (čužój).

parole.significato: The twenty-sixth letter of the Russian alphabet, called ша (ša) and written in the Cyrillic script. The letter sound is…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic Ⱎ (Š), then from Hebrew ש or Coptic ϣ (š) or Arabic ش (š).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic шьствие (šĭstvije), from Proto-Slavic *šьstvьje. Constructed from the root of Proto-Slavic *šьdlъ (resultative participle, later past tense, of *jьti (“to go”)) + *-ьstvo + *-ьje (compare Russian идти́ (idtí), -ство (-stvo), -ие (-ije)).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic шьствовати (šĭstvovati). By surface analysis, ше́ств(ие) (šéstv(ije)) + -овать (-ovatʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic шлѣмъ (šlěmŭ), from Proto-Slavic *šelmъ. Doublet of шело́м (šelóm), the inherited East Slavic form.

parole.significato: generous (willing to give and share unsparingly)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic щедръ (štedrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ščedrъ. The expected form would be *щёдрый (*ščódryj), compare Belarusian шчо́дры (ščódry). Cognate to Polish szczodry and Ancient Greek σκεδάννῡμι (skedánnūmi, “I split or scatter”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ѫдоль (ǫdolĭ), from Proto-Slavic *ǫdolь. Doublet of удо́ль (udólʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic юноша (junoša), from Proto-Slavic *junoša. Compare Old East Slavic уноша (unoša).

parole.significato: young, youthful (in the early part of life or growth)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic юнъ (junŭ), from Proto-Slavic *junъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *jauˀnás, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuh₁en-. Displaced the inherited Old East Slavic унъ (unŭ), оунъ (unŭ).

parole.significato: yus, either of two letters, little yus (Ѧ) and big yus (Ѫ), representing nasal vowel sounds in the old Cyrillic alphabe…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ѫсъ (ǫsŭ, “big yus”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic генварь (genvarĭ), генуарии (genuarii), from Byzantine Greek Γενάρης (Genárēs), Ἰανουάριος (Ianouários), from Latin Iānuārius, from Latin Iānus (“god in Rome mythology”), from (perhaps) Proto-Indo-European *ei- (“to go”).

parole.significato: differently, in a different way; otherwise
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *jьnako. Comparative degree of either Old East Slavic инакъ (inakŭ), Old East Slavic инако (inako) or Old Church Slavonic инакъ (inakŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic искусьство (iskusĭstvo), which was either inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьzkusьstvo, or an inner formation from искоусъ (iskusŭ, “test, experiment”) + -ство (-stvo).
